REPORT 
The Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) are rightly hailed as „the temples of modern India.‟ 
They were conceived to be a critical component of our mixed economy and were put into 
operation for transforming the independent India into a modern and industrially advanced nation. 
Primacy given to the CPSEs arose out of the fact that the private enterprises were not adequately 
equipped to undertake the mammoth task of creating infrastructure and other facilities which 
were indispensable for nation -building. The contribution of PSEs towards the growth of Indian 
economy through measures such as generation of income, capital formation, generation of 
employment, development of infrastructure facilities, building a strong industrial base, export 
promotion and impor t substitution, contribution to central exchequer, removal of regional 
disparities, checking concentration of income & wealth etc. is really commendable. 
 The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in India 
2. The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE s) comprise enterprises established by the 
Government of India (GOI) as Government companies under Section 617 of the Companies Act, 
and wherein the equity holding of the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It also includes statutory 
corporations constituted und er specific statutes of the Parliament. The CPSEs do not, however, 
include departmental undertakings, banking institutions and enterprises where equity holding of 
the GOI is 50% or less.  
3. The number of CPSEs has increased from 5 during the first five ye ar plan to 366 as on 
31.3.2020. The cumulative investment (paid up capital plus long term loans), which was Rs. 29 
crore in 5 enterprises as on 31.03.1951, has gone up to Rs.  20.62 lakh crore in 366 CPSEs.  Out 
of these 366 CPSEs, 256 are in Operation, 96 CPSEs have yet to commence business and 14 are 
under liquidation or approved for closure. Out of 256 operating CPSEs as many as 171 CPSEs 
showed profit during 2019 -20, 83 CPSEs incurred losses during the year, and 1 CPSE had no 
profit no loss. The Central Public Sector Enterprises are under the administrative control of 
various Ministries/ Departments and decision with regard to major investments, expansion, 
diversification, joint ventures, modernisation, technology upgradation, etc. are taken by the 
CPSEs in consultation with their respective administrative Ministries/Departments. 
 Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) 
4.      In their 52nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3rd Lok Sabha (1962 -67) stressed the 
need for setting up a centralized coordinatin g unit, which could also make continuous appraisal 
of the performance of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public 
Enterprises (BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of the 
reorganization of the Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE 
was made part of the Ministry of Industry. In May, 1990, BPE was made a full fledged 
Department known as the DPE. Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public 
Enterprises (Mo HI &PE).                            
 

2 
 
5.      The DPE is the nodal department for all the CPSEs and formulates policy pertaining to 
them. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, 
autonomy and financi al delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It further collects and 
maintains information in the form of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of 
CPSEs.        
6.      In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinates with other Min istries, CPSEs and 
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the 
following subjects have been allocated to the DPE: 
 Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public-Sector Enterprises.  
 Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial 
Management Pool. 
 Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the 
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism. 
 Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of  Arbitration for the Public -Sector 
Enterprises.  
 Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector 
Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and other 
capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises 
including the mechanisms therefore. 
 Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises. 
 Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises. 
 Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises including conferring „Ratna‟ status. 
 Survey of Public Enterprises. 
7.      According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises the Vision and Mission statements of DPE are as follows: 
 Vision 
 “Effective, Profitable and Globally Competitive Central Public Sector Enterprises” 
 Mission 
  “To continuously improve management and performance of CPSEs through Corporate 
Governance, Performance Evaluation, Human Resource Management, Research & Development 
so as to enhance their global competitiveness” 
 
 
 

3 
 
 Impact of Covid-19 and the Lockdown on CPSEs 
8. The impact of Coid -19 pandemic on India has been largely disruptive in terms of 
economic activity and loss of human lives.  CPSEs have been no exception to the adverse impact 
of the pandemic & subsequent lockdowns.  CPSEs being the maj or thread in the socio-economic 
fabric of the country, it has to witness unprecedented challenges like temporary shutdown, 
reduced scale of operation and production, manpower shortage, supply chain disruptions, 
restricted logistics and transportation etc.,  posed by the ongoing Covid -19 pandemic, on the 
operations and production capacity of the CPSEs.

10. The Committee is deeply concerned about the adverse impact of Covid -19 pandemic 
on CPSEs and the huge losses suffered by almost all the af oresaid CPSEs in the 1 st  and 2nd  
quarter of the financial year 2020 -2021 as compared to that of the previous financial year.   
The Committee hopes that the CPSEs would be able to overcome this situation through the 
various initiatives undertaken to mitiga te the adverse impact and improve their 
profitability in the financial year 2021-22.   
11. The information submitted by DPE regarding categorization and autonomy of CPSEs is 
as under:-  
Categorization of CPSEs 
12.  CPSEs are categorized into four schedules  namely „A‟, „B‟, „C‟ & „D‟ based on criteria 
such as quantitative parameters, i.e., Investment, Capital Employed, Net Sales, Profit before Tax, 
Number of employees and units, Capacity Addition, Revenue per employee, Sales/Capital 
Employed, Capacity Utiliz ation, Value added per employee as well as qua litative  parameters, 

4 
 
i.e., National importance, Complexities of the problems being faced by the company, Level of 
technology, Prospects of expansion and diversification and competition from other sectors are t o 
be considered while examining such proposals. In addition, critical/strategic importance of the 
concerned CPSE as well as factors such as Share price, MoU ratings, Ratna status, ISO 
certification are also taken into consideration. 
13.        The present procedure of categorization of CPSEs involves consideration of the 
proposals in the administrative Ministry concerned and the Department of Public Enterprises 
which consults the Public Enterprises Selection Board. The categorization of CPSEs has 
implications mainly for organizational structure and salary of Board level incumbents of the 
concerned CPSE. It also plays a role in grant of autonomy to the Board s of CPSEs under „Ratna‟ 
scheme. A s informed by DPE, at present there are 66 Schedule „A‟, 65 Schedule „B‟, 44 
Schedule „C‟ and 5 Schedule „D‟ CPSEs. The schedule -wise list of CPSEs is given in 
Annexure-I.                                                                                          
   Autonomy of CPSEs 
14.     The endeavor of the Government is t o make Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
autonomous board managed companies. Under Articles of Association, the Board of Directors of 
CPSEs enjoys autonomy in respect of recruitment, promotion and other service conditions of 
below board level emplo yees. The Board of Directors of a CPSE exercises delegated powers 
subject to broad policy guidelines issued by Government from time to time. The Government has 
granted enhanced powers to the Boards of the profit -making enterprises under various schemes 
like Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna by delegating powers in the areas of (i) capital 
expenditure, (ii) investment in joint ventures/subsidiaries, (iii) mergers & acquisitions, (iv) 
human resources management, etc.  
15. The main objective of the Maharatna s cheme which was introduced in 2010 is to 
empower mega CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants. The Maharatna 
Scheme empowers big sized CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants.The 
Government had introduced the Navra tna scheme, in 1997, to identify Central Public Sector 
Enterprises (CPSEs) that had comparative advantages and to support them in their drive to 
become global giants.  In October 1997, the Government had decided to grant enhanced 
autonomy and delegation of financial powers to some other profit making companies subject to 
certain eligibility conditions and guidelines to make them efficient and competitive. These 
companies, called Miniratna, are in two categories, namely, Category - I and Category -II. As 
informed by DPE, p resently there are 10 Maharatna CPSEs, 14 Navratna CPSEs and 73 
Miniratna CPSEs (61 Miniratna category-I and 12 Miniratna category-II) (Annexure-II).

17.      The Committee notes that as per the provisional data provided by the DPE, the 
number of CPSEs has increased to 366 (from 348 in 2019)  with a total investment of Rs. 
20,61,857 crore (an increase of 29.7%)  as of December, 2020. Out of this 366 CPSEs, 256  
are operational CPSEs (earlier it was 249, an increase of 7  CPSEs). Out of 25 6 operational 
CPSEs, 171 are profit making, 83 incurred losses. As on December, 2020 the overall  
networth of all CPSEs was Rs 12.14 lakhs crores. The overall net profit of operating CPSEs 
was Rs 1.38 lakh crores. Further, most of the indicators such as paid -up-capital, Capital 
employed, Net Worth, Investment, Total Turnover etc. indicate a steady inc rease from 
2017-18 to 2020-21. 
18. However, indicators such as profit of profit making CPSEs, contribution to Central 
Exchequer, Foreign exchange earnings etc. have shown decline compared to the previous 
year.  Even though the number of operating CPSEs has  increased from 249 to 256, the no. 
of regular employees in CPSEs has reduced from 10.7 lakh in 2018 -19 to 9.2 lakh in 2019 -
20. Therefore, there has been a reduction of 1.5 lakh regular employees in the 256 
operating CPSEs, as compare d to the previous year . DPE has informed that the reduction 
in the number of regular employees is due to VRS opted by BSNL employees.  The 
Committee is deeply concerned to note the continuous decline in the number of regular 
employees in CPSEs, year after year, for the past several years.  
19. The main purpose of setting up of PSEs was to achieve various socio -economic 
objectives such as higher economic growth, self reliance in production of goods and 
services, employment generation etc.  
 

6 
 
20. The Committee therefore, recommends that DPE should monitor the compliance of 
their directions issued  to all Ministries/Departments to sensitise CPSEs to put in place a 
system of „Succession Planning‟ to ensure that all vacant critical positions of CPSEs are 
filled through regular incumbents , rather than by casual/contract employees . The 
Committee may be apprised of the action taken by CPSEs to put in place a system of 
succession planning.  The Committee further reiterates its earlier recommendation that 
DPE should act as a watchdog to ensure  timely filling up of all vacancies arising from time 
to time, rather than putting the onus on the administrative Ministries/Departments alone.

Scheme of  Research, Development and Consultancy (RDC) on Generic issues related to 
Public Sector Enterprises : 
31.    The Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) was 
introduced in the year 2007 -08 and is being implemented since 2008 -09. In view of instructions 
issued by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) with regard to rationalization of Schemes, the  Scheme 
for Skill Development/Training programme to executives/employees of State Level Public 
Enterprises (SLPEs) was merged with the Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector 
Enterprises (PSEs) during the year 2016-17. 

10 
 
32.    RDC scheme was modified so that activities could be spread round the year and its scope 
was expanded and diversified to include more activities. Some of the features of revised scheme 
are elaborated as under: 
        i.          Thematic studies and consultancies on generic is sues like corporate governance, 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, professionalization, project management, risk 
management, human resource management, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) etc. related 
to Public Sector Enterprises are undertaken. I n addition, benchmarking studies on selected

MoU System for CPSEs 
64.    The Government of India introduced the MoU system in the year 1986, based on the 
recommendations given by Arjun Sen Gupta Committee Report (1984) . The report 
recommended that the CPSEs should enter agreement with their administrative Ministries for 
five years, with progress to be reviewed annually. The MoU system was given broader thrust by 
the Governments after the announcement of the New Industrial Policy of 1991. 
65.    DPE monitors and evaluates the profitability and efficacy of MoU signing CPSEs 
through their MoU targets & their evaluation to measure the performance of the management of 
the CPSEs on key selected parameters so as to improve the critical performance indicators of the 
organization. 
66.    MoU guidelines are reviewed from time to time based on the feedback received from 
Administrative Ministries/ CPSEs and based on the changes occurred in the Regulations. 
67. Some of the main points  of the latest MoU Guideline issued by DPE on 17th January, 
2019 are as under:- 
1. Memorandum of Understanding: MoU is a negotiated agreement and contract between 
the Administrative Ministry/Department/ Holding CPSEs i.e. majority shareholder and the 
Management of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE) on selected parameters having 
targets decided normally before the start of a new financial year and results evaluated af ter the 

20 
 
end of the year to measure  the performance. MoU system involves target set ting in financial and 
non- financial areas and performance evaluation of those targets. 
2. Purpose of MoU:  The purpose of the MoU is to measure the performance of the 
management of the CPSEs on key selected parameters against the targets agreed upon so as to 
improve the critical performance indicators of the organisation. 
3. Scope: All CPSEs (Holding as well as Subsidiaries) are required to sign MoUs. The 
Holding companies will signMoUs with their administrative Ministries/ Departments, while the 
Subsidiary companies will sign MoUs with their respective Holding companies. 
 
4. Exemption from MoU:The following CPSEs are exempted from MoU system: 
 
i.     CPSEs under liquidation where Liquidator has already been appointed. Administrative 
Ministry would provide the list of such CPSEs. 
ii.       CPSEs which are not in operation or having no employees or on any other ground on 
the recommendation of administrative Ministry with approval of InterMinisterial 
Committee or High Powered Committee. 
5.     Parameters: CPSEs work in various sectors under different conditions. In view of this, the 
following guidelines are laid down:- 
5.1    For 50% weightage, t here would be uniform parameters for measuring financial 
performances such as revenue from operations, operating profi t and return on investment (e.g. 
ratio of PAT/Net -worth). This would be applicable to all CPSEs, except CPSEs which are 
dependent on government grant or performing functions of distribution of grant etc. e.g. 
Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Coun cil (BIRAC). Hence, 3 financial parameters 
have been prescribed for all CPSEs with total weightage of 50% except for CPSEs like BIRAC. 
5.2    For the remaining 50% weightage, a menu of parameters has been suggested for selection 
depending on the sector in which the CPSE is operating. Separate Format has been given for 
Finance Sector and another Format for the remaining operating CPSEs. The parameters most 
appropriate and relevant for measuring performance shall be suggested by the Pre -Negotiation 
Committee (PNC) to the Inter -Ministerial Committee (IMC). In all the cases IMC shall take 
appropriate decision on the suggestions made by PNC. 
5.3    Chairman, IMC is authorised to modify the parameters or weightages of parameters in 
sector specific cases, if justified. 
6. High Powered Committee (HPC) : The High -Powered Committee (HPC) is the Apex 
body under MoU system for laying policy guidelines, approval of the benchmarks and indices 
recommended by IMC.   
7. Pre-negotiation Committee (PNC):  The role of the Pre -negotiation Committee (earlier 
known as Standing Committee on MoU) would be to assist IMC in determining the most 
appropriate and relevant parameters for measuring improvement in performance and for fixing 
targets. Meetings of the Pre -negotiation Committee wou ld be held in each case before the 
meetings of IMC to look at the trends, discuss, negotiate and recommend MoU parameters and 

21 
 
targets. The Pre -negotiation committee comprises Adviser (MoU), DPE, concerned Joint 
Secretary/Adviser of Administrative Ministry, concerned Adviser (NITI Aayog), Director (MoU) 
and representative from Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI). 
8. Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) : MoU targets are decided by the IMC. Inter -
Ministerial Committee on MoU consists of Secr etary, DPE as Chairman, Secretary of concerned 
administrative Ministry/Department or his representative not below the rank of Joint Secretary 
(Member), Secretary, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation or his representative 
not below the rank of Joint Secretary (Member), Additional Secretary, NITI Aayog or his 
representative (Member). Secretary, DPE may co -opt any officer who is a finance expert in case 
the need is felt. 
9. Time-lines for submission of MoU:  The draft MoU with all documents/ Ann exures 
should be submitted to administrative Ministry/ Department in respect of all CPSEs and their 
subsidiaries by 21st November of each year for the forthcoming year. The draft MoU after the 
approval of administrative Ministry/ Department should be sent to DPE by 15th December of 
each year for the forthcoming year with all documents/Annexures. Administrative Ministry/ 
Department would ensure that the targets are realistic, growth -oriented, aspirational and 
consistent with the latest Annual Plan, Budget and Corporate Plan of the CPSEs. 
10.   MoU Signing Process :MoU based on the parameters, targets and weightage 
recommended by IMC without any deviation shall be signed between CMD/ MD of CPSE and 
Secretary of administrative Ministry/ Department in case of holding/ independent CPSEs and 
between CEO/ MD of subsidiary company and CMD/ MD of holding CPSE in case of subsidiary 
by 31st March (i.e. before start of financial year in respect of which targets are fixed) or within 
21 days from issue of IMC meeting minutes, whichever is later. In case, deviation is detected, 
IMC minutes would prevail. 
11.   MoU Evaluation: Evaluation of MoU of the CPSE is done after the end of the year on 
the basis of actual achievements vis -à-vis the MoU targets. CPSEs (Holding as well a s 
Subsidiaries) are required to submit performance evaluation reports on the basis of audited 
accounts to Department of Public Enterprises after approval of the Board of CPSE and through 
the administrative Ministries/Departments on or before 30th September  (in respect of 
immediately preceding year) or any other date communicated by DPE. Figures and information 
in the MoU achievement which are not verifiable from audited accounts would be relied on the 
basis of certification by way of resolution of the Board given separately for each parameter. 
12. MoU Score  and  Rating:  MoU  score  is  an aggregate of score on all parameters with 
respect to performance vis -à-vis the targets. With a view to distinguish „excellent performance‟ 
from „poor performance‟, five d ifferent performance ratings have been fixed in the MoU, i.e., 
„Excellent‟, „Very Good‟, „Good‟, „Fair‟, and „Poor‟.  
13. CPSEs not signing of MoU or not submitting MoU evaluation:  The CPSEs who do 
not submit Draft MoU/ MoU evaluation through their adminis trative Ministries/ Departments 
within a stipulated time of the prescribed date will be rated as „poor‟. Stipulated time would be 
decided by Secretary, DPE (presently stipulated time is six months vide OM no M -

22

Revival/ Restructuring/ Closure and Disinvestment of CPSEs 
 
72. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for the l osses/ sickness in CPSEs. The 
Department in their written submission informed that some common problems for sickness in 
CPSEs include old and obsolete   plant  and machinery, outdated technology, low capacity 
utilization, low productivity, poor debt –equity structure, excess manpower, weak marketing 
strategies, stiff competition, lack of business plans, dependence on government orders, heavy 
interest burden, high input cost, resource crunch, etc. Further with privatization, liberalization 
and opening up of the economy, those CPSEs which did not change along with the fast -changing 
times lost ground to private companies and turned loss making and sick.  
 
73. The Committee hopes that the I nter Ministerial consultative process, together with 
DPE's role as a mentor  and guide would facilitate the incipient sick and weak CPSEs into 
taking mid -term course , corrections so that they are saved from entering into the 'sick' 
bandwagon and likewise the 'weak' CPSEs would be able to nurse t hemselves back into 
good financial health.  
 
74. The Government has taken many steps to make the mechanism and process for revival/ 
restructuring of CPSE time bound, comprehensive, performance driven and efficient.  The 
Government has decided to remove multiple layers in the decision making p rocess to ensure 
timely revival/ restructuring of sick CPSEs. It has been decided that revival/restructuring of sick/ 
incipient sick CPSEs is to be merit based taking into account strategic, national and business 
concerns of the CPSE. 
 
75. The DPE had on 2 9th October, 2015 laid down guidelines for streamlining the 
mechanism for restructuring/ revival or closure of sick or incipient sick CPSEs and weak CPSEs 
which were revised on 07th September 2016. Further, on 14th June 2018, DPE again issued 
revised guidelines on „time bound closure   of  sick/loss making CPSEs and disposal of movable 
and immovable assets. These replace the earlier guidelines issued by DPE on this subject. 
 
76. The guidelines are intended to expeditiously complete the procedures for closure  of 
CPSEs and lay down responsibilities   of the concerned Ministries/ Departments/ CPSE, etc., 
including the support required to be extended by nodal Departments/ Organizations like, 
Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog, etc. The revised guidelines prescribe a matrix of timelines for 
step by step process to be completed in respect of a CPSE under closure and about disposal of its 
assets. The guidelines on time bound closure of sick/ loss making CPSEs uniformly provide for 
payment of VRS/VSS at 2007 notional pay scale to employees of CPSEs under closure 
irrespective of the existing pay scales of the company.

Disinvestment 
80. The Committee is aware of the fact  that the Finance Minister has set a Disinvestment 
target of Rs.1.75 lakh crores  for the current financial year . The FM  unveiled the Public Sector 
Enterprises ( PSE) Policy for Atmanirbhar Bharat and announced that barring four strategic 
sectors, Public Sector Enterprises in other sectors will be divested.  The following sectors are 
specified as strategic sectors:- 
 
(i) Atomic Energy, Space and Defence; 
(ii) Transport and Telecommunication; 
(iii) Power, Petroleum, coal and other miners; and 
(iv) Banking, Insurance and Financial Services.  
81. The Committee sought the details of   the role of DPE in operationalising and achieving  
the disinvestment targets set for the year 2021 -22. The DPE informed that Department of 
Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) is the nodal Department for the New Public 
Sector Enterprises Policy on CPSEs, disinvestment and asset monetization of C PSEs and their 
implementation. The subject matter does not come under the purview of DPE. DIPAM on 04 th 
February, 2021 has issued operational modalities of the New Public Sector Enterprises policy. 
82. Besides, the Secretary in his deposition before the Co mmittee, while making presentation 
on the Demands for Grants 2021 -22, had stated that in order to get a better return on the 
investments of a CPSE, the governm ent sometimes has to go for  disinvestment which exposes 
the company to a wider competition in the market. Such competition provides the Company, a 

25 
 
 platform for a turnaround for the better. Accordingly, some CPSEs that are even profit making 
are being disinvested, while others that are loss making, but cater to strategic sector may not be 
disinvested. 
83. The Committee is of the view that all efforts should be made to infuse the requisite 
capital into the CPSEs, so as to enable them to stand shoulder to shoulder with the private 
entities and offer stiff competition to them. The Committee feels that CPS Es had always 
played a vital role in unbundling privitisation sin ce a long time and thus deserve  the much 
needed support. 
84. The Committee's view is that CPSEs are the backbone of the economy and there 
should be no stone left unturned to strengthen the CP SEs that are profit making and 
adding their contribution to the nation economic kitty.  The Committee also desires that it 
be apprised of the reasons as to why the reviving and restructuring mechanisms failed to 
have any positive effect on the loss making CPSEs.  
85. The Committee is of the opinion that DPE should have a mechanism in place to 
ensure that all their guidelines being issued from time to time are complied with by the 
CPSEs/Administrative Ministries/Departments.   The Committee notes that the 
Government has set a disinvestment target of Rs. 1.75 lakh crores and has decided to divest 
all PSEs which are not in the four strategic sectors identified by DIPAM, M/o Finance.  The 
Committee may be apprised of the revised mechanism for time bound closure o f loss 
making CPSEs and disposal of assets, once it is finalized.  The Committee also notes that in 
the coming years, more number of CPSEs in the non -strategic sectors and strategic sectors 
(except those in the four areas identified) will be divested/priva tized/merged/closed.  
Therefore, the number of employees likely to opt for VRS is also likely to increase.  
Therefore, Department should for esee this scenario and take appr opriate measures timely 
to impart their skill training under CRR Scheme to enable them to get re-deployment.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
 
95. As per Section 135 of the Com panies Act, 2013, all profit making corporates, including 
CPSEs exceeding threshold limits  prescribed in the Act having  net worth of Rs. 500 crore, or 
turnover of Rs. 1000 crore or net profit of Rs. 5 crore, are mandated to spend at least 2% of the 
average net profits (Profit Before Tax) of the company made during the three immediately 
preceding years to undertake CSR activities. Such companies have to constitute a CSR 
committee of the Board, comprising three or more Directors with at least one Independent 
Director. 
  
96. The Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 notified by M/o Corporate Affairs and the 
Schedule VII of the Act lists the activities that can be undertaken under CSR. An advisory on 
observance of transparency and due diligence in selection and imp lementation of activities under 
CSR was issued by Department of Public Enterprises to the CPSEs in August, 2016. The 
Department has also issued guidelines on 10.12.2018  to all administrative Ministries & CPSEs 
for adopting a theme -based focused approach ev ery year on CSR expenditure by CPSEs. These 
guidelines inter alia provide that CSR expenditure for such thematic programmes should be 
around 60% of annual CSR expenditure of CPSEs. The aspirational districts identified by NITI 
Aayog may be given preference . The theme for 2019 -20 was School education, Healthcare and 
Nutrition and the theme identified for the FY 2020- 21 is „Health and Nutrition‟.

various developmental works/schemes for the benefit  of North Eastern Region and Sikkim. 
The Committee is further aware that the NER expenditure under Central Sector Schemes 
are being monitored every quarter jointly with M/o Development of NER to improve 
utilization of funds for NER under the Schemes. 
(Para 55) 
18. The Committee notes that for the Financial Year 2018 -19, both BE & RE allocation 
for RDC & CRR Schemes in the North -Eastern Region stood at Rs. 0.85 c rore.   Since AE 
was also Rs. 0.85 crore, DPE could utilize the entire amount during that year fo r RDC and 
CRR Schemes. 
(Para 56) 
19. However, during 2019 -20, AE was only Rs. 0.53 crore though both the BE & RE 
were Rs. 0.95 crore.  Therefore, DPE could spend only 56% of the allocated amount during 
the Financial Year 2019 -20.  During the Financial Year  2020-21, Rs. 1.05 crore was 
allocated as BE which was reduced to Rs. 0.56 crore at RE stage.  However, no expenditure 
was made under NER for both the Schemes during Financial Year 2020 -21, as no trainings 
could be conducted due to COVID -19 Pandemic.  For the Financial Year 2021 -22, Rs. 0.85 
crore has been allocated under NER for RDC & CRR Schemes.  Therefore, the Committee 
suggests that DPE should resume the trainings and conduct programmes in physical as well 
as virtual mode. The Committee is also of the view that under the CRR Scheme, all efforts 
should be made to identify more number of VRS optees/dependents in NER and  impart 
training to them to enhance their scope for redeployment.  Similarly, under the RDC 
Scheme also, more number of training programmes and workshops should be conducted to 

34 
 
enhance the optimum utilization of allocated budget even though the funds get transferred 
to non-lapsable pool, without getting lapsed. 
(Para 57) 
20. The Committee notes that CAPEX is an important component for moder nization 
expansion and diversification of CPSEs thereby improving the productivity of PSEs as well 
as economic growth of the country.  The Committee therefore suggests that DPE may 
continue to monitor the implementation of CAPEX activities of CPSEs regular ly.  DPE 
may also conduct more number of capacity building workshops on MoU System to sensitise 
CPSEs to leverage their net worth for CAPEX, as CAPEX is included as one of the 
parameters in the MoU evaluation system. 
(Para 62) 
21. The Committee further rec ommends that DPE should take appropriate steps to 
achieve the planned target of capital expenditure by CPSEs to revive the economy from the 
fallout of Covid-19 Pandemic.  
(Para 63) 
22. The purpose of MoU is to measure the performance of management of CPSEs  on 
key selected parameters against the targets agreed upon so as to improve the critical 
performance indicators of the organization.  It is an important tool being used by DPE for 
evaluating and monitoring the performance of CPSEs.  The Committee notes th at the 
number of MoUs signed during the Financial Year 2019 -20 and 2020 -21 was 144 and 124 
respectively. 
 
(Para 70) 
23. The Committee appreciates the new initiative taken by DPE to have a new 
framework for MoU System using a digital platform/dashboard for a self -driven MoU 
mechanism for the target setting and performance evaluation of CPSEs.  The Committee 
hopes that with the implementation of the New Framework and a digital dashboard with a 
centralized portal for entering, signing, monitoring and evaluatin g MoU agreements, the 
MoU System will be more simplified and transparent. 
(Para 71) 
24. The Committee hopes that the I nter Ministerial consultative process, together with 
DPE's role as a mentor and guide would facilitate the incipient sick and weak CPSEs i nto 
taking mid -term course , corrections so that they are saved from entering into the 'sick' 
bandwagon and likewise the 'weak' CPSEs would be able to nurse t hemselves back into 
good financial health.  
(Para 73) 

35 
 
 
 25. The Committee notes with concern that a  sizeable amount of land assets of CPSEs 
under closure are lying unsold/not transferred. The Committee recommends that DPE may 
use its good offices to impress upon the concerned administrative ministries to arrive at 
quick decisions so that these lands  could be utilized for useful purposes so as to become 
gainful and beneficial for the society at large, besides creating employment opportunities 
for the youth.  
(Para 79) 
26. The Committee is of the view that all efforts should be made to infuse the requisite  
capital into the CPSEs, so as to enable them to stand shoulder to shoulder with the private 
entities and offer stiff competition to them. The Committee feels that CPSEs had always 
played a vital role in unbundling privitisation sin ce a long time and thus deserve the much 
needed support. 
(Para 83) 
27. The Committee's view is that CPSEs are the backbone of the economy and there 
should be no stone left unturned to strengthen the CPSEs that are profit making and 
adding their contribution to the nation economic kitty.  The Committee also desires that it 
be apprised of the reasons as to why the reviving and restructuring mechanisms failed to 
have any positive effect on the loss making CPSEs.  
(Para 84) 
28. The Committee is of the opinion that DPE should have a me chanism in place to 
ensure that all their guidelines being issued from time to time are complied with by the 
CPSEs/Administrative Ministries/Departments.  The Committee notes that the 
Government has set a disinvestment target of Rs. 1.75 lakh crores and has decided to divest 
all PSEs which are not in the four strategic sectors identified by DIPAM, M/o Finance.  The 
Committee may be apprised of the revised mechanism for time bound closure of loss 
making CPSEs and disposal of assets, once it is finalized.  Th e Committee also notes that in 
the coming years, more number of CPSEs in the non -strategic sectors and strategic sectors 
(except those in the four areas identified) will be divested/privatized/merged/closed.  
Therefore, the number of employees likely to op t for VRS is also likely to increase.  
Therefore, Department should foresee this scenario and take appropriate measures timely 
to impart their skill training under CRR Scheme to enable them to get re-deployment. 
(Para 85) 
29. The Committee observes that  p rofessionalization of Boards of CPSEs plays a 
significant role in ensuring good corporate governance thereby promoting CPSEs to be 
more dynamic, competitive, performance oriented and viable in the market driven 
economy.  However, it is quite disheartening to note that around 480 positions of Non -
Official Directors (NOD) and 128  posts of senior officers including Functional  Directors 
are lying vacant on the Boards of various CPSEs as on date. The presence of NODs in the 

36 
 
Boards of CPSEs is essential to impro ve the functioning and effectiveness of the Board and 
to safeguard the interests of all stakeholders. 
(Para 91) 
30. The Committee strongly objects to the failure on the part of DPE to furnish the 
information regarding vacant posts of Directors to be filled  by PESB.  DPE brings out the 
Public Enterprises Survey every year & is also the nodal Department of all CPSEs.  Under 
such circumstances, DPE should have been prudent enough to make available  the 
information to the extent available, to the Committee for perusal. 
(Para 92) 
31. The Committee is dismayed by the increase in the number of vacant positions of 
Non-Official Directors of CPSEs from 313 in 2019 -20 to 480 in 2020 -21. Despite repeated 
recommendations made by the Committee in this regard, the Departmen t has not been 
proactive enough to get the huge number of vacant posts  filled up  which has a negative 
bearing on the effective functioning of the CPSEs.   The Committee feels disappointed by  
the inordinate delay in filling up such important positions, putti ng the effective functioning 
of CPSEs at stake.  The Committee therefore, recommends that DPE should play a more 
pro-active role and ensu re that vacancies of Directors o n the Boards of CPSEs do not 
remain vacant for more than six months  as any laid back ap proach in these matters would 
only jeopardize the growth of CPSEs as a whole.  The Department should desist in putting 
the complete onus on the Administrative Ministry/Department of the CPSEs or PESB.  The 
Committee further reiterates its earlier recommenda tion to include this as a parameter for 
MoU evaluation of CPSEs and impose penalty on such CPSEs wh ich do not fill up vacant 
posts of Directors in the Boards of CPSEs timely.  DPE should also chalk out a strategy to 
monitor the status of filling up of vaca ncies by the Search Committee/PESB/Management 
of CPSEs (in respect of below Board level posts). 
(Para 93) 
32. The Committee further recommends that a detailed exercise through a professional 
agency to assess the current status of implementation of various Human Resources (HR) 
development issues /activities in CPSEs should be conducted and best practices be 
identified  and replicated in CPSEs, as had been done by the Department earlier. 
(Para 94) 
33. The Committee is aware that under the Section 135 of the Co mpanies Act, 2013, 
CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) activities have been made mandatory for all profit 
making CPSEs to allocate 2% of their average net profits (NBT) of the three preceding 
years. Further as per the latest guidelines issued by the DPE vide their OM dated 10 th 
December, 2018, the CPSEs are to utilise the CSR Fund in a focussed manner towards 
national priorities by adopting a theme based approach each year. The Committee  
understands that most of the contributions to the PM CARES Fund by t he CPSEs have 
been made from their CSR Funds diverting a large share that would have otherwise been 
utilised towards theme based CSR activities in the local areas.   The Committee therefore, 

37 
 
desires that the CSR Fund should be utilised to meet the targets s et for the theme based 
activities in the respective area and aspirational districts as spelt out in the guidelines. 
(Para 100) 
34. The Committee notes that CSR expen diture during the year 2019 -20 wa s much 
higher i.e. Rs. 5066.93 crore than the previous Fin ancial Year 2018 -19.  The Committee 
suggests that the CPSEs should utilize the CSR fund mainly for undertaking activities 
related to „Health & Nutrition‟, the theme identified during Financial Year 2020 -21, for 
focused intervention by CPSEs under CSR.  The Committee further recommends that DPE 
should also maintain information regarding the activities undertaken by CPSEs under 
CSR fund as it is a parameter for MoU evaluation & DPE is the nodal Department for all 
CPSEs.  Further, M/o Corporate Affairs may be impressed upon to involve local 
representatives in the project selection.  The Committee further is of the view that a set of 
statutory rules/guidelines may be framed or incorporated in the current rules ibid wherein 
it becomes mandatory to seek the opinion  of the local area representative before 
finalizing/implementing a scheme under CSR. The Committee is also of the view that more 
number of training programmes on CSR should be included in the RDC Scheme to enable 
CPSEs to undertake the right kind of activities under CSR.  
(Para 101) 
35. The Committee further recommends that CPSEs should fulfill the social objective of 
removing regional disparities in the count ry and should, therefore, also focus  their CSR 
expenditure in geographically remote and backward areas of the country, in addition to the 
Aspirational Districts. The Committee further desires that CPSEs should use their 
innovative ideas and management skills for environmental protection.  
(Para 102) 
36. The Committee observes that the Department has tak en initiatives to conduct 
studies in diverse areas. However, the Committee is surprised to note that no study has 
been conducted to assess the impact of Covid -19 on CPSEs, despite the fact that DPE is the 
nodal Department of all the CPSEs.  The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion 
that a detailed study needs to be conducted to comprehend at micro-level, the actual impact 
of COVID -19 pandemic and subsequent lockdowns on the performance of the CPSEs so 
that necessary in tervention by the Governme nt could  be made to mitigate the economic 
fallout.  
 (Para 104)

 1 
REPORT 
 
The Union Budget 2021 -22 has been unfolded in the backdrop of the severe economic fallout 
wrought by the global Pandemic.  For a year now, the Country was under the clutches of Covid -19 
Pandemic and consequent lock-downs causing disruptions in the economic activities across all sectors.  
With a view to reboot the economy, the initiative “Atmanirbhar Bharat” was envisioned to address 
the damage wreaked by the pandemic.  The sui generis Budget thus , aims to the manifestation of 
Atmanirbhar Bharat by i ncreasing self-reliance and India's ability to become a global manufacturing 
hub across sectors by promoting domestic enterprises & indigenous technology.  The focus of the 
Budget are health & well -being, physical and financial capital and infrastructure b uilding, inclusive 
development, reinvigorating human Capital, innovation and R&D and minimum government and 
maximum governance.  
 
2. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and 
examined the Demands for Grants (2021-22) of the Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy 
Industries and Public Enterprises) in its meeting held on 19th February, 2021. 
 
Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) 
 
3. The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) under the Ministry of Heavy Industries an d Public 
Enterprises promotes the development and growth of three sectors i.e., Capital Goods, Automobile and 
Heavy Electrical Equipment in the country and administers 29 Central Public Sector Enterprises 
(CPSEs) & 4 Autonomous Organizations.  The CPSEs un der the Department manufacture a wide 
range of products viz., Boilers, Gas/Steam/Hydro Turbines, Industrial Machinery, Machine Tools, 
Turbo Generators and Consumer Products such as Paper and Salt.  The Department supports the 
development of a range of Inte rmediate Engineering Industry such as Castings, Forgings, Diesel 
Engines, Tools and Dies Industrial Gears and Gear Boxes.  
 
4. The Department Provides oversight to the following autonomous organizations: 
 
(i) Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI); 
  (ii) Fluid Control Research Institute (FCRI) 
  (iii) NATRIP Implementation Society (NATIS); 
  (iv) Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI). 
 
5. The objective of the Department also includes maintaining  constant dialogue with various 
Industry Associations in the  Capital Goods, Automobile and Heavy Electrical Equipment Sector and 
encourages initiatives for the growth of industry in these areas.  The Department also assists the 
industries in achieving their growth plans through policy support, an d other interventions such as 
advocating rationalization of tariff, promoting technological collaboration & investment, research & 
development activities etc.,

Overview of the Automotive Industry 
 
13. The Indian Automobile Industry comprising automobile and the automotive component 
segments is one of the key contributors to economic growth of India. Being deeply integrated with 
other industrial sectors, it is a major driver of the manufacturing Gross Domestic Product (GDP), 
exports and employment. India is a prime destination for many multinational automobile companies 
with the aspirations of business expansion , and t he basic advanta ges that the country provides as an 
investment destination, includes cost-effective operations, efficient and large-scale manpower, a fast 
growing dynamic market, since the liberalization of the sector in 1991 , and allowing 100%  FDI 
through automatic route. In Indian Automobile Sector today, there is presence of almost every global 
auto manufacturer in the country. All categories of vehicles like Two Wheelers , Three Wheelers , 
passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, trucks, buses, tractors, Heavy commerci al vehicles etc. are 
produced in India. India is the largest manufacturer of Two Wheelers  and Three Wheelers and the 
fourth largest manufacturer of passenger cars in the world. Further, the manufacturing of automobiles 
including trucks, buses, cars, three wheelers/two wheelers etc, has risen at a very high pace  in India. 
Indian Automobile Industry today is  a `7.2 lakh crore industry. Presently, the a utomobile industry 
turnover constitutes 6 - 7% of GDP, 27% of Industrial GDP and 49% of Manufacturing GDP and  
provides about 8 million direct and 29 million indirect employments. Besides the current annual sale 
of vehicles is about 26 milli on and 8% of the total exports worth `1.94 lakh crore come from the 
automobile industry. It is also a large contributor to th e national exchequer, contributing Rs.1.5 lakh 
crore in the total GST which corresponds to 13% of the total GST collection.   
 
14. The Indian Automobile Industry contributes in an immense way to the Agricultural Sector of 
the country owing to the fact that  agricultural Machinery mainly consists of Agricultural Tractors, 
Power Tillers, Combine Harvesters and other Agriculture Machineries & Implements.  Due to 
negligible production of Power Tillers, Combine Harvesters and other Agricultural Machineries, this 
Sector is mainly dominated by Agricultural Tractors.  Indian Tractor Industry is the largest in the 
world (excluding sub 20 HP belt driven tractors used in China), accounting for one third of the global 
production.  The other tractor markets in the world a re China and United States.  Indian Tractors were 
exported to the US and other countries like Malaysia, Turkey, etc.  Indian players have aggressively 
started exporting to African countries.  Indian Tractors are gaining acceptance in international markets.  
As the cost of tractors in India is the cheapest in the world, there is tremendous scope for improvement 
of export of tractors in future.

National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP) 
. National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP) is the largest and one 
of the most significant initiative s of the Government of India in the Automotive sector so far and 
represents a unique joining of hands between the Government of India in Department of Heavy 
Industry, a number of State Governments and Indian Automotive industry to cre ate a state -of-the-art 
Testing Validation and R&D infrastructure in the country.  The Project envisaged upgrading two 
centres at ARAI, Pune and VRDE Ahmednagar and setting up of 4 Centres of state-of-the-art testing 
and homologation at ICAT/Manesar, GARC/Chennai, NATRAX/Indore, and NIAMIT/Silchar.  Under 
NATRiP, the following centres have been set up:- 
 
 International Centre for Automotive Technology (ICAT), a full -fledged testing and 
homologation centre within the northern hub of automotive industry at Mane sar in the 
State of Haryana; 
 
 Global Automotive Research Centre (GARC) a full -fledged testing and homologation 
centre within the southern hub of automotive industry at a location near Chennai in the 
State of Tamil Nadu. 
 
 Up-gradation of existing testing an d homologation facilities at Automotive Research 
Association of India (ARAI), Pune and at Vehicle Research and Development 
Establishment (VRDE), DRDO, Ahmednagar; 
 
 National Automotive Test Tracks (NATRAX), world -class proving grounds, testing 
tracks in Indore, Madhya Pradesh; 
 
 National Institute for Automotive Inspection Maintenance and Training (NIAIMT), 
National Specialized Hill Area Driving Training Centre as also Regional In-Use vehicle 
management Centre at Dholchora (Silchar) in the State of Assam. 
 
16. In accordance with the approval of CCEA, NATRiP has completed 21 of the 22 sanctioned 
facilities.  Some of the facilities created under NATRiP of various centres are given below: 
 ICAT, Man esar – Passive Safety Lab, Powertrain Lab, EMC Lab, Fatigue Lab,

 GARC-Chennai – Fatigue Lab & Certification Lab, Test Tracks, CAD/CAE Lab &

 NATRAX-Indore – Powertrain Lab, Vehicle Dynamics Lab, CAD/CAE Lab and Test

 VRDE, Ahmedanagar – Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) Lab & ABS Test Track. 
 
 NIAMIT, Silchar – Training Test Tracks, Model I&M, Mechanics Training Institute

Faster Adoption & Manufacturing of (Hybrid &)  Electric Vehicles in India (FAME – India) 
Scheme Phase-II 
 
25. The Department of Heavy Industry notified Phase -II of the Scheme, vide S.O. 1300 dated 8 th 
March, 2019.  Phase-II of the Scheme is for a period of 3 years, commencing from 1 st April, 2019, 
with  an outlay of `10,000 crore.  The main objective of the scheme is to encourage faster adoption of 
Electric and hybrid vehicles by way of offering upfront Incentive on purchase of Electric vehicles and 
also by establishing the necessary charging Infrastructure of electric vehicles.   
 
 
 Salient feature of FAME India Scheme Phase-II 
 
 Outlay of `10,000 Crore for 3 year 
 
 Aims to generate demand by way of supporting 7090 e -Buses, 5 lakh e -3 Wheelers, 
55000 e-4 Wheeler Passenger Cars (including Strong Hybrid) and 10 lakh e-2wheelers. 
 
 Emphasis on providing affordable & environment friendly public transportation options 
for the masses, the scheme will be applicable mainly to ve hicles used for public 
transport or those registered for commercial purposes for all segments of vehicles. 
 
 Applicable to only those EVs which are fitted with advanced chemistry batteries. 
 
 Applicable to only those vehicles which is defined as Motor Vehicl e as per CMVR and 
eligible to be registered with the Road Transport Authority. 
 
 Demand incentive is linked to battery capacity i.e., `10,000/KWh for all eligible 
Vehicles except e-Buses (for which the incentive is `20,000/KWh) subject to capping at

36. As part of examination of the DFG 2021 -22, some of the Automobile Association had 
submitted before the Committee the following concern s and challenges facing the Industry that 
requires attention of the Government.  The Committee recommends that DHI may suitably 
intervene with the Ministries concerned for addressing these issues: 
 
 Acute shortage of steel being supplied by domestic suppliers, leading to increase in 
steel prices in the Country. 
 
 Acute shortage of containers and significant increase in price of international 
logistics. 
 
 Mandatory certification of some of the components like Safety Glass (for QCO) 
has been enforced.  The implem entation of QCO for Safety Glass has  been

 Implementation of Quality Control Orders (QCOs) and BIS licensing for auto

 Hardships being faced due to delay in customs c learance post implementation of

 Surge in price because of implementation of BS-VI emission norms. 
 Shortage of semiconductor and chips 
 To make Dealer's entire Auto Business (Dealership + Workshop) a part of MSME. 
Presently only 2 wheeler and passe nger vehicle dealers workshops are under 
MSME. 3 wheeler, commercial vehicle, tractors and construction equipment 
categories also needs to be included in MSME category. 
 
 Need of Auto Zone to redress the issue of Land Classification.  Presently 
showroom lan d is considered as commercial land and Workshop land is 
considered as Factory land.  There are many Dealerships where showrooms and 
workshops are together and hence they face the brunt of local authorities in terms

37. The Committee has been informed by the Auto Associations that the fast -tracking of 
emissions and fuel efficiency in India has resulted in large investments and cost increase.  
Further the two big regulations which include CAFE Phase 2 and BS VI phase 2 are to be 
implemented from April, 2022 and April, 2023 respectively. These regulations will have major 
economic impact leading to further cost increase affecting adversely the already stressed 
automobile industry.   The per capita  income of our  country has not increased in the same 
tandem as the increase in cost.  It was further informed that t he Indian fuel emission standards 
are now equivalent to standards of many automobile manufacturing countries globally  and the 

 17 
fuel emission levels have gone down and also the fuel efficiency has improved significantly.  The 
Auto Associations, therefore, suggested for deferment of the following emission regulations.  The 
Committee, with a view to boost the struggling Automotive Sector, the following suggestions of 
the Automobile Associations for  temporary deferment in the emission regulations is forwarded 
for consideration of the Government: 
 BS VI Phase 2 Emission regulations, including RDE and PEMS which are notified 
for implementation from 1 st April, 2023 may be deferred to 1 st April, 2024 for new 
models and 1st April, 2025 for existing models. 
 
 Phase 2 Fuel Efficiency Regulations for Passenger Vehicles notified for 
implementation from 1 st April, 2022 may be deferred  for implementation from 1 st 
April, 2024. 
 
 Fuel Efficiency Regulation for Light, Medium and Heavy - Duty BS VI vehicles may 
also be implemented from 1st April, 2024. 
 
 OBD II Regulation for two Wheelers and three Wheelers scheduled for 1 st April, 
2023 may be deferred and implemented in two phases, 1 st Phase from 1st April, 2024 
and 2nd Phase from 1st April, 2026. 
 
38. The future of the automobile Industry is going to be influenced by the next generation 
autonomous driving technology.  The next generation autonomous driving technology is  
currently in the development and testing phase in the developed nations. It would rather 
enhance road safety and reduce road accidents, pollutions and carbon emissions, fuel 
consumption, road congestion , make transportation accessible to all including dis abled. The 
Committee has been informed that the autonomous vehicles are in different levels, with level 0 
being the manual cars of today and level 5 the fully autonomous, self -driven vehicles.  The 
Committee is aware of  a few demerits of autonomous vehicles in Indian environment owing to 
the heavy traffic and poor road conditions, more so as it will affect the employment of Drivers.  
In India, some manufacturers are now introducing level 1 autonomous vehicle.  OEMs are 
working on R&D and would be launching different levels of vehicles with autonomous 
functionality in the near future.  The Indian automobile industry has a stake on the global Auto 
Sector and hence any lag may leave us behind in the race. To keep pace with the latest 
technology, the Committee e xpects that necessary initiative  in this regard is taken  to promote 
autonomous driving technology to compete with the international market trends.   
 
39. The GST rates on automobiles are at the highest level  of 28% .   Indian industry and 
suppliers have inv ested significant resources to migrate to BS -VI.  As far as two -wheelers are 
concerned, in leapfrogging from BS -IV to BS-VI, Industry has recorded a 35% increase in cost 
in the last quarters.  Small engine size two -wheelers are used by a major population o f self -
employed, entrepreneurial common people.  Hence there is need to consider the affordability for 

 18 
end-customer.  Reduction in GST rate would help sustained growth in the industry and 
accelerate the adoption of BS-VI and improve GST collection accruing from increased sale.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that to improve affordability of the customers and 
simultaneously boost the automobile sector, the GST rate on all segments may be reduced from 
28% to 18%. The decreased GST rate would prove to be  an impetus to enhance the sales and 
thereby, would offset the losses, if any, to the Exchequer kitty. 
 
40. Of late , the Government has announced the much-awaited voluntary vehicle scrapping 
policy to phase out old polluting vehicles. It is said that  with the approval of scrapping policy, 
India will become an automobile hub  and t he recycled material from old vehicles will  help 
reduce prices .   DHI in their written reply has informed that as per the Ministry of Road, 
Transport and Highways, the scrapping po licy would cover an estimated 51 lakh Light Motor 
Vehicle (LMVs) that are above 20 years of age, b esides another 34 lakh LMVs that are above 15 
years.  It would cover 17 lakh medium and heavy motor vehicles which are above 15 years.  
Hence the scrapping policy would give an impetus to sales in the automotive industry.  However, 
the Auto Associations are of the view that the scrapping policy will not work without fiscal 
incentives in the form of rebates in GST, road tax and registration changes.  The details  of the 
policy are yet to be released. The Committee is in agreement with the suggestion of  the Auto 
Associations and urges for inclusion of fiscal incentives in the policy like rebates in GST, road 
tax and registration charges as done in the case of EVs  in states  like Delhi ,  to encourage 
replacement of old  vehicles with newer ones.

opportunities. Besides, a Phase II of the Scheme has been submitted to the Ministry of Finance as a

recommended that the Scheme fulfils the technological and infrastructural requirements of the Capital 
Goods Sector in a limited way and the Scheme needs up -scaling by at  least 10 times in physical and 
financial terms to create the desired impact.

requirements when scaling-up needs. The Committee notes that the M/o Financ e have provided

Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI) 
 
71. Central Manufacturing Technology Institute, a premier R&D organization in the manufacturing 
technology, established in the year 1962, is an autonomous body. The institute is assisting Indian 
Industries to achieve excellence in technology and stimulate economic growth. The Institut e is active 
in metal working technology, evolving solutions to national strategic initiatives and is a one -stop 
destination for end -to-end solutions in manufacturing technology deployment. The Institute is guided 
by a Governing Council consisting of repres entatives from industries in the manufacturing sector, 
machine tool manufacturers, Government nominees and other stakeholders. 
72. CMTI supports the Indian engineering industry and various sectors through its value-added 
services in manufacturing technolog y and product development/realization activities. It continues to 

 29 
play a vital role of a catalyst in the application of manufacturing technology. The Institute is equipped 
with trained manpower, equipment and facilities for design, research, prototype prod uction, 
manufacturing, testing, inspection, calibration, product development, training and technical 
information. 
73. Over the years CMTI evolved as Centre of Excellence for Machine Tool and Manufacturing 
Process Development; developed special purpose machines for various needs and significantly assisted 
MSMEs by providing high value added services. This has been possible with in -house capabilities 
covering the entire product development cycle viz., ideation, design, manufacturing, testing of pilot 
plants, and system integration in related areas. Today, CMTI undertakes research, develops process 
technologies and machines, trains manpower and deploy the solutions to applications. The focused 
domains include Ultra - precision machine tools, Special purpose mach ines, Sensors and machine 
controls, Textile machineries, Smart manufacturing and Industry -4.0 enabled technologies, Additive 
and other special manufacturing processes, Precision Metrology, Aircrafts LRUs including test rigs 
development & qualifications, Sk illing and Reskilling (experienced learning). There are about 35 
technologies which are ready for licensing to industrial use and to manufacture in multiple. CMTI also 
hand- holds the technology licensee and the start -ups through incubation/consultancy, un til 
commercialization of acquired technology. 
CMTI has successfully developed: 
 Five planetary mixing machines of various capacities (upto 4.5 tonne) for different 
customers. 
 The High speed shuttleless rapier loom developed by CMTI has been successfully 
tested for waiving range of cotton and polyester yarns. 
 Sensor Technology development facility and Nano manufacturing facilities having 16 
clean room facilities have been created. 
 CMTI in its endeavour to develop smart machines has developed smart ultra -precision 
diamond turning machine built in with several intelligent features. Under the aegis of 
‘Samarth Udyog’ initiative for Industry 4.0 of DHI, CMTI is establishing “Smart 
Manufacturing Development and Demonstration Cell” with the consortium of six 
industries. While Smart Factory is being established, 11 IIoT solutions relevant to metal 
cutting industries have already been developed for the benefit of MSMEs. 
 CMTI has contributed significantly towards Linear Electrohydraulic Servo Actuators 
(LESA) indigenous  efforts of Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA). CMTI has  
designed test rigs and established the protocols for three categories of LESA actuators. 
These have been successfully handed over to ADA on 16th August 2019. The LESA 

 30 
actuators developed indigenou sly for LCA -TEJAS aircraft have undergone successful 
flight tests at supersonic speed on 28th May 2020. 
 Compact Air Bearing Rotary stage, Temperature sensors, IIoT module for energy 
monitoring in CNC machines are important machine tool aggregates developed  at 
CMTI in the current year.

that DHI may pursue the matter vigorously with the Ministry of Finance for approval of Pha se-
II proposal and apprise the Committee of the outcome.  
(Para 58) 
 
24. The Committee appreciates the efforts undertaken by the DHI regarding promotion of 
technological development and innovation and suggests that a master list of all the imported 
items used by CPSEs in assembly of their products should be prepared and shared with all the 
national research centres and educational institutions indulged in R&D activities, design and 
scientific innovations. Further the Committee desires that such research ins titutions should be 
provided financial assistance to support R&D activities for creation of a healthy manufacturing 
ecosystem. 
(Para 60) 
 
25. The Committee notes that DHI is developing web -based open manufacturing Technology 
Innovation Platforms under the ongoing Capital Goods Scheme for enhancing India’s 
technological capabilities. The Committee hopes that this initiative would facilitate more start -
ups and angel funding of innovations in India as well as development of mother manufacturing 
technologies in digenously through Grand Challengers on the Platform. The Committee 
recommends that the six Technology Platforms which are presently under trial runs may be 
formally launched on priority to promote industrial investments. Further, the Committee 
recommends that DHI should take all out efforts to promote the development of Technical 
Platforms under the Capital Goods Scheme in order to ensure their optimum utilization by 
experts including academia, technology students, manufacturing experts, etc. 
(Para 61) 
 

 48 
26. The Committee appreciates the new initiative taken by DHI for constitution of Project 
Development Cell (PDC)  for attracting investments and development of investible projects in 
India in coordination with various other Ministries/Departments and State G overnments. 
However, the it is observed that the efforts made by DHI have not been able to achieve tangible 
results for  large -scale investment.  The Committee, therefore, desires that the DHI should 
explore new avenues and also equip the PDC to cater a better coordination and wider outreach.  
(Para 63) 
    
27. It has been stated that the project had been delayed due to several reasons as there were a 
number of First time activit ies. The most important reason wa s the need for steam turbine 
design updation , as a result of design review by an international ly reputed organization  in 
Germany. The steam turbine wa s being designed by BHEL for the first time, and a number of 
improvements and additional studies were  identified as a result of the said design review. A 
number of Indian and foreign consultants have been appointed to realise a reliable design. The 
target date for completion was to end by September 2020. However, this got impacted  due to 
Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent lockdown.  The entire allotted fund for the project has 
already been released by the Government in the FY 2020-21.    DHI, in its written reply, have 
stated that the AUSC Project achieved its physical closure on 31 st December 2020 and that its 
financial closure is scheduled on 31 st March 2020. The Committee notes the efforts put in by 
DHI together with its flagship PSU, i.e BHEL, NTPC, IGCAR and the DST in completion of the 
AUSC Project, despite facing a number of hurdles and failing of meeting targeted timelines. The 
Committee desires that the Ministry along with other stakeholders may come up with more such 
technology projects so that power efficiency is improved and emissions get reduced.  
(Para 66) 
   
28. The Committee express es its displeasure over the poor utilization of the allocated fu nds 
for development of Industry Association and PSUs for undertaking promotional activities.  
Analysis of the utilization trend under this account for the past years, reveals that the 
expenditure has been made sparsely in spite of scanty allocation  too. Today wide publicity and 
awareness hold key for beneficiary to tap the benefit of the schemes of the Government available 
for promotion of manufacturing and technological avenues of Capital Goods Sector.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Departm ent should seek more funds for 
promotional activities and at the same time pro-actively utilize the entire allocation by arranging 
effective promotional activities in large numbers to create vast awareness of the benefits of 
Capital Goods Sector. 
(Para 70) 
 
29. While going through the history of allocation to CMTI, the Committee observes that the 
funds allocated over the years in BE has not been adequate to meet the actu al expenditure of the 
Institute, thus necessitating the need for allocation of enhanced RE every year. The Committee is 
perturbed to observe the poor under-utilization by the Department in the current financial year, 
which had a good track record of utilizing the fund optimally for the R&D activities of CMTI.  
The Committee, therefore, strongly believes that the Department will leave no stone unturned in 
utilizing the entire balance fund in the FY 2020-21. 
(Para 75) 
 
30. The Committee observes that the operating CPSEs , this  year has come down to 17 from 
22 in the  previous year and further t wo more CPSEs viz., Scooters India Ltd. (SIL) and Bharat 

 49 
Pumps and Compressors Ltd. (BPCL) have also been approved for closure by the CCEA.  The 
Number of Profit making CPSEs have also come down to six this year from 10 in  the previous 
year. The Committee expresses its concerns over the poor performance by the CPSEs , which 
also reflects the  DHI’s unsuccessful endeavour to  extend proper support and handholding to 
those CPSEs slipping into loss  mode. The Committee recommends that DHI should undertake 
periodical performance evaluation of each CPSEs and extend the required supportive 
intervention from time to time in enhancing the capacity building capability of the sick and 
incipient sick CPSEs. 
(Para 83) 
 
31. The Committee was informed that PSUs viz Bridge and Roof Ltd., ha s outstanding dues 
to the tune of `74.25 crores towards MSMEs for the goods and services received from them. The 
Committee recommends that Government may direct the PSU concerned to ensure that the 
pending dues to the MSMEs are released exp editiously. The Committee also desires to be 
updated of the action taken in this regard. 
(Para 84) 
 
   32. The Committee also recommends that the DHI should monitor the CPSEs under its 
administrative control to ensure timely payment to MSMEs i.e., within 45 days from the date of 
acceptance of goods and services from them  in compliance to the stipulation announced by the 
Government under the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan. 
(Para 85) 
    
33. BHEL a Maharatna Company which had a high turnover and profit making PSU  has 
slipped into loss making  since FY 2019-20.  BHEL has immense potential to cater to indigenous 
production.   The Committee takes note of the efforts put in by BHEL as well as the innovative 
measures taken to combat Covid -19 and developed/manufactured products such as (i) 
BHELMister (equipment for mass sanitization), (ii) Electrostatic Disinfection Machine for 
disinfection/sanitization of offices, hospitals etc., (iii) Full Body Sanitization Chamber etc. The 
Committee is of the view that BHEL should als o take initiatives to cut its fixed costs and 
diversify beyond power into areas like defence, transportation, aerospace, e -mobility batteries, 
oil & gas etc. for revenue generation post -Covid-19 Pandemic to achieve the vision of 
Atmanirbhar Bharat and become a Global engineering organisation. 
(Para 86) 
 
34. The Committee notes that 40% of the component required for HMT Machines viz. CNC 
Controllers & Drivers, Spindle Bearings, Linear Motion Guides etc were imported.  However, 
disruptions in import due to lo ckdowns and closure of ports have adversely affected the 
productions. Efforts have been made by HMT to provide technical support to Domestic 
Manufacturers and utilize its infrastructure facilities for production of import substitutions. The 
Committee recommends that new avenues may be explored for alternate manufacturing hubs 
for import substitution and technology transfer from other countries to meet the requirements 
of HMT so that the production process is back on track.   
(Para 88) 
 
35. The Committee not es that in October, 2018 the Government had approved the Revival 
and Mill Development Plan (RMDP) of NEPA Ltd. which was slated to be completed in 

 50 
December, 2019 with a total financial package of `469.41 crores. However, the RMDP missed its 
first deadline and, as intimated by DHI, was likely to be completed in September, 2020 as it has 
been designed to boost production and support/generate local employment.  On completion of 
RMDP, NEPA is expected to produce 1,00,000 MT p.a. of Writing & Printing Paper and 
Newsprint paper which will help minimise imports and increase exports. Since the lockdown has 
been eased almost completely, the manpower and other facilities are available for carrying out 
RMDP works in full swing.  DHI had apprised the Committee that a Mo nitoring Committee 
under the Chairmanship of AS&FA, DHI has been constituted to regularly review the progress 
of the implementation of the RMDP. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should 
be made on a priority basis to complete the RMDP of NE PA expeditiously. A compliance report 
on this aspect may be furnished to the Committee. 
(Para 90) 
  
36. The Committee notes that BPCL has imposed a ban on Capital Expenditure to manage 
its cash crunch caused due to the Covid -19 Pandemic lockdowns. However,  with the opening of 
lockdown, economic activities have resumed in a large scale improving the earnings. The 
Committee is of the view that as the Capital Expenditure is a critical driver for economic growth 
and employment generation; BPCL should strive to meet its targeted Capital Expenditure set for 
the FY 2020-21. 
(Para 92) 
 
37. The Committee recommends that DHI should make concerted efforts to relieve the 
company from its dependency on Chinese raw materials and co -ordinate with concerned Indian 
stakeholders, who are able to provide the Company with adequate raw-materials, so as to enable 
the Company to engage in production seamlessly and realise the vision of an ‘Atmanirbhar 
Bharat’. 
(Para 94) 
 
38. The Committee notes with distress that in the dilly -dally approach of the stakeholders, 
the performance and efficiency of HEC is deteriorating and resulting into the Company 
incurring further losses. The Committee is apprehensive that, if this lethargic attitude continues, 
then HEC is likely to face the same fat e as other PSUs decided for closure. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that DHI should vigorously pursue the matter with all the 
stakeholders concerned for revival/re-structuring of HEC expeditiously.  
(Para 96) 
 
39. The Committee desires to be  updated about the status and action taken by the 
Department with regard to the following CPSEs which have been considered/approved for 
closure/disinvestment/ transfer/merger and long pending for final settlement/closing: 
 (i) Bharat Pumps & Compressors Ltd., 
 (ii) Scooters India Limted 
 (iii) HMT Machine Tools Ltd. 
 (iv) Hindustan Paper Corporation Ltd. 
 (v) Nagaland Pulp & paper Corporation 
 (v) Hindustan Newsprints Ltd. 
 (vi) Sambhar Salts Ltd. 

 51 
 (vii) BHEL-EML 
 (viii) Hooghly Printing Co. Ltd. 
 (ix) Engineering Projects (India) 
(Para 97) 
 
40. The Committee desires that  DHI may take corrective and co ercive action to infuse more 
working capital into these loss making CPSEs, provide more B2B interface between CPSEs and 
clients, to enhance order bookings, bri ng in handsome and attractive VRS/VSS compensation 
schemes in co -ordination with DPE and encourage them to replace their obsolete machinery 
with new and state-of-the-art ones so as to nurse them back to good financial health. 
(Para 99) 
 
41. The Committee n otes that most of the contributions to the PM CARES Fund by the 
CPSEs have been made from their CSR Funds , thus  diverting a large share that would have 
otherwise been utilized towards theme based CSR activities in their local areas. The Committee 
recommends that efforts should be made to ensure that the CPSEs utilize their CSR Funds 
particularly during the Covid -19 Pandemic fully to meet the targets set for the theme based 
activities in their respective areas, in consultation with the local Representatives of the area  
(MLA, MLCs, MPs). 
(Para 101) 
 
42. The Committee is aware that under the Public Procurement Policy (PPP), the MSEs are 
promoted to improve their market accessibility and competitiveness through increased 
participation in Government procurements and encouraging development of linkages between 
MSEs and PSEs. As per the mandate of the Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) Order 2012, every Central Ministries/PSEs should set an annual target of 
minimum 25% procurement of go ods & services from MSE Sector. Out of 25% annual 
procurement, a sub -target of 4% & 3% should be from MSEs owned by SC/ST and Women 
entrepreneurs, respectively. Keeping in view the extraordinary situation, the Committee is of the 
view that the PSUs may pro cure more than the prescribed limits laid down und er the PPP for 
MSEs Order 2012 from the MSEs, especially the SC/ST and women owned MSEs, so as to give 
further boost to the localised production and fulfilment of the PM’s vision of an ‘Atmanirbhar 
Bharat’. 
(Para 102)
