FAME (India) - I Scheme 
17. The Ministry of Heavy Industries informed the Committee that FAME India 
(Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid & ) Electric Vehicles in India 
Scheme was launched on 1 st April, 2015 for a period of two years with an outlay of 
795 crores intended to  support the hybrid/electric vehicle market development and 
its manufacturing eco -system to achieve self -sustenance.  The Scheme is one of the 
green initiatives of the Government of India to promote hybrid/electric technology in 
Road Transport so as to red uce dependence on fossil fuels as well as reduction in 
Green House Gas (GHG) emissions. Phase-I of the Scheme was extended from time 
to time upto 31st March, 2019 with an enhanced outlay of 895 crores.   
18. In the First Phase of the Scheme , about 2.8 lakh  hybrid and electric vehicles 
were supported by way of demand incentive amounting to 358 crores  (Approx.) 

8 
 
resulting in saving of about 84 million litres of fuel and reduction of about 210 
million Kg of CO 2 as on 31 st May, 2021. The Scheme further supported  deployment 
of 425 Electric buses in about 9 cities by way of incentives amount to 280 crores 
(Approx).  Through these buses, an additional 80 million litres of fuel and about 180 
million kg of CO 2 is expected to be saved during the lifetime of bus.  Proje cts were 
sanctioned for setting up of 520 charging stations to the tune of 43 c rores (Approx.) 
in cities like Bengaluru, Chandigarh, Jaipur and NCR of Delhi and major highways 
such as Delhi -Chandigarh, Mumbai -Pune, Delhi -Jaipur, Delhi -Agra etc.  Out of 
these 520 Charging stations, 392 charging stations have been installed.  Based on the 
outcome and experience of the phase -I of the Scheme, Phase-II of FAME India was 
approved by the Government and notified on 8 th March, 2019.

19. The 2nd Phase of FAME Scheme commenced from 1 st April, 2019 with an

PLI Scheme 
23. India has been heavily reliant on the international market to meet its electric 
vehicle ( EV) component needs, especially battery cells. Pre sently, Lithium-ion 
chemistry based battery is popular in electric vehicles. Since India doesn’t have 
manufacturing facility for Lithium ion battery cells, all battery cells used for battery 
pack in electric vehicles are imported. Localization of cell manu facturing will , 
therefore, help in reducing EV costs, and in achieving self -sufficiency in EV growth.  
A national level strategy to secure critical raw material sources for cell 
manufacturing, and to incentivize local cell manufacturing through capital sub sidy, 
favour trade and FDI Policy, and investment models such as PPP are the  way 
forward to "Make in India". 
24. Accordingly, a Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for manufacture of 
Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India has been approved by the Union Cabinet 
on 12 th May, 2021 in order to enhance India’s Manufacturing Capabilities and 
Enhancing Exports – for manufacture of Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India, 
The total outlay of the ACC PLI is Rs.18,1 00 crores for 5 years. The PLI Scheme for 
ACC ba ttery envisages incentivizing large domestic and international players in 
establishing a competitive ACC battery set -up in the country. It represents one of the 
largest economic opportunities of the twenty -first century for several global growth 
sectors, s uch as consumer  electronics, electric vehicles  and renewable energy.  The 
PLI Scheme for ACC batteries describes ACCs as battery cells with new generation, 
advanced storage technologies that can store electric energy as chemical energy and 
convert it back t o electric energy when required. The plan proposes a           
production-linked subsidy based on applicable subsidy per KWh and percentage of 
value addition, achieved on actual sales made for manufacturers who set up 
production units with a capacity of at least 5 GWh.

MAJOR CHALLENGES IN SMOOTH & FASTER EV ADOPTION 
 
64. The EV adoption challenges differ from country to co untry depending on 
various factors such as Per Capita Income of consumers (Purchasing Power), Price 
Sensitivity of the consumers, Unique Conditions, EV Infrastructure development & 
readiness of local EV parts Manufacturing Ecosystem etc. In the case of Ind ia, EV 
adoption is more difficult as compared to many other countries.   The main 

25 
 
challenges expressed by auto associations and vehicle manu facturers are delineated 
in the succeeding paras:- 
 
Affordability and Demand Generation 
65. The biggest challenge in the EV adoption is the affordability, demand creation 
and high upfront cost. Affordability in Indian conditions is very different from the 
rest of the world as per capita income in India is only about USD 2000, about 5% of 
that in Europe and Japan. This reduces the ability of many people to buy higher 
priced cars. As a result, 77% of cars sold  in India are less than 4 metres in length 
with average Ex -Showroom price is only Rs 6.6  lakhs and only 5% of cars sold  in 
India are priced at  Rs.15 lakhs or  more. Currently, t he cost of an EV is twice the 
price of an Internal Combustion Engine ( ICE) car. Even for a small car, it is 
estimated to be in the range of Rs. 12 -16 lakhs. Therefore, penetration of EVs at this 
price point is likely to be slow. 
66. The Committee notes that the EV industry  is initially facing many 
challenges for take -off due to poor demand from consumers owing to high 
upfront cost of EV s in comparison to I nternal Combustion Engine (ICE)  
vehicles, inadequate charging infrastructure etc. The Committe e urges the 
Government to play an important role as a catalyst for enabling faster adoption 
of Electric Mobility through  subsidies, incentives and long -term sustainable 
policies for demand creation. Further, S tates which have not fully waived off 
road tax/registration fee on EVs should be directed to do so in order to attract 
consumers to go for EVs. Lowering the price of EVs and additional incentives 
on scrapping ICE vehicles for EVs can also fast-track transition to Electric 
Mobility. 
Range Anxiety of Customers & Lack of Charging Infrastructure. 
67. Consumers have high sensitivity towards charging time, travel distance on full 
charge and the availability of charging infrastructure. This is collectively known as 
range anxiety. Robust charging infrastructure  is the basic and predominant 
requirement for Electric Mobility.  Due to rising petrol prices and low running cost 
of Electric Vehicle, middle cla ss families are considering buying electric vehicle. 
However, lack of visibility of public charging infrastruc ture creates dilemma in the 
minds of consumers for making purchase decision of electric vehicles, which has 
been one of the major challenges in the transition to Electric Mobility. 

26 
 
68. Customers are also apprehensive of limited range provided by current EV s as 
it compels the customers to stick to intra -city journeys only and not inter -city trips. 
As per Deloitte survey, 35% consumer think drivi ng range as the major constraint in  
buying EV.

Non-availability of EV Components and Lack of Local Supply Chain. 
72. There is  lack of an integrated EV eco -system. An integrated EV Industrial 
cluster ensures a sustainable supply of batteries and other critical component s such 
as semiconductors, powertrain control systems and driving motor. EV has three 
critical components  - Batteries, Motor and power electronics. All these are high 
investment products. In addition, parts such as PCB, LCD/LEDs, Capacitors, 
Resistors, Diodes, Switches, Transistors, Connectors, Relays continue to be imported 
from china, Taiwan and South Korea. 90% of the world’s manufacturing of 
advanced Chemistry Cell  (ACC) is done in China.  USA, Europe and South Korea

84. The Committee was informed that Fin ance for retail consumers of EVs is still 
difficult and at higher cost. EVs are regularly charged higher interest and insurance 
premium than ICE Vehicles. Moreover, specia lized EV finance options are limited. 
Availability of easy and affordable financing options wo uld encourage EV Purchase.

vehicle’s value is well -understood, making loans secure for the bank. However, 
this is not the case with EVs, as their residual value is not clear. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should designate EV as a 
priority len ding sector, especially financing for commercial fleets, as they are 
critical to the transition towards cleaner mobility. Availability of easy loans 
with lower interest and longer tenures will make it easier for the consumer to 
go for EVs, which ultimately  lead to faster adoption of electric mobility across 
the country.

customers in terms of Products, Solutions and the Technology advancement that has

customers apprehensive on the choice and hesitate to consider them as an option. 
Hence, a robust public  awareness campaign on the benefits of EVs, economic 
affordability and the latest technology being deployment may help allay such fears 
and improve the customer perception towards the EV segment.

stakeholders (especially manufacturers) should make use of every feasible 
promotional and advertising platform to highlight the benefits of Electric

Investment (RoI) and cost of ownership benefits of EVs vis a vis conventional 
Internal Combustion Engines (ICE) can be demonstrated. Customers may also 
be educated about the various benefit s, incentives and subsidies offered by the 
Government such as exemptions of EVs from road tax during vehicle 
registration, discounts offered on purchase of EVs etc.

local EV Parts manufacturing eco-system that is at global scale and quality.

Ministry for technological advancement. The spending in  India on R&D is

infrastructure to promote indigenous manufacturing to reduce import s and

on creating local manufacturing ecosystem at global scale in order to lower the

manufacturing eco-system that is at global scale & quality.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE – AT A GLANCE 
 
1.  The Committee notes that India being the fifth largest automobile 
market in the world, imports crude oil from  outside to cover 80% of its 
transport fossil fuel, thereby dra ining public exchequer and also increasing 
pollution from traditional I nternal Combustion Engine Vehicles is at alarming 
levels. The Committee  further notes that India’s EV Ecosystem is still a t a 
nascent stage, as compared to several other count ries in the world.  Therefore, 
the need of the hour is to scale up the transition process to electric mobility. The 
Committee welcomes the decision take n by the Govt. of India to switch over to 
Hybrid & E lectric Vehicles to tackle the GHG (CO2)  emissions from transport 
sector, helping to reduce crude oil import and also be in line with the latest 
global technology. 
(Para 11) 
 
2. The Committee notes that Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEV s) comple ment 
Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) by not only contributing to meet key national 
objectives of reducing fossil fuel consumption and carbon emissions by 
replacing Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles but also in speeding up 
BEV adoption as both these technologies have common EV parts. The 
Committee further notes that since the Hybrid vehicles use dual power train the 
gross weight is higher resulting in relatively lower efficiency, in comparison to 
EVs.  
(Para 16 (i)) 
 
3. The Committee further notes that BEV enjoys some distinct advantages.  
Firstly, the electricity cost associated with operating a BEV over one mile is 
significantly lower than the gasoline cost required for operating a comparable 
ICE Vehicle over the same distance.  Secondly, BEV costs less to mainta in, 
owing to the relative elegance and simplicity of a battery -electric motor system 
compared with the frequent maintenance required for operation of an ICE.  
Further, given the high tank -to-wheel efficiency of EVs, overall CO 2 emissions 
per vehicle will r emain lower than ICEs.  The trend towards a higher share of 
renewable energy in energy generation will  further make EVs even more CO 2 
efficient. The Committee , therefore, hopes that the EV Sector in India will 
witness growth in the coming years, with more consumers opting to adopt EVs. 
 
(Para 16 (ii)) 

39

Industries in Phase -II of the Scheme, in order to accelerate the transition to 
Electric Mobility. India primarily being a Two -Wheeler (2W)  driven market

decision under FAME -II scheme to increase the subsidy/incentive from Rs.

(Para 22 (ii))

active charging stations ins talled all over the country and the locations readily 
available for the consumers for their reference enabling them to easily track the 
nearest charging station at times of need while on the move.  The Committee , 
therefore, urges that the MHI in coordinati on with the Ministries/Agencies 
concerned, may put in place such a facility for enhancing the e -Mobility 
services. 
 
(Para 71 (iv)) 
 
24. The Committee desires that for increasing numbers of charging stations, 
the Government may explore installing Smart Mete rs on electric Poles  at 
dedicated locations and make small charging stations across the 
city/villages/highways and issue smart cards to the EV owners, who can charge 
their batteries anywhere which can be a good booster for faster adoption of 
EVs. 
 
(Para 71 (v)) 
 
25. The Committee further recommends that expenditure incurred on setting 
up of charging stations may be brought under the ambit of CSR for a limited 
period of 2 -3 y ears.  Further, renewal energy may be used for powering the 
Public Charging Stations. 
(Para 71 (vi)) 
 
26. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Government needs to 
forge international partnerships to secure access to key minerals.  The 
Government may form consortium for joint research, investment pooling and 

45 
 
development of battery technology and battery recycling.  Since India is already 
a global powerhouse in information technology, communication, digital 
technologies, an excellent foundation may be set up for the development of 
cutting-edge battery management systems.   
(Para 78) 
 
27. Home to some of the most polluted cities on the earth, India is pivoting 
towards new-energy electric vehicles to clean up its toxic air. But with meager 
resources of lithium, the mineral essential to make batteries for electric 
vehicles, it is having to scout for resources overseas. India’s EV production will 
rely heavily on imports from China of  lithium chemicals used to make 
cathodes and battery cells  as China has a thriving lithium chemical, battery 
cathode, battery cell and EV supply chain. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Government should explore other sources of battery raw 
material like Lithium etc. rather than solely relying on China for its import 
needs to ensure unhampered supply of raw materials.  
(Para 81) 
 
28. The Committee further recommends that Government should endeavour 
to achieve self -dependency in manufacturing Lithium -ion batteries to reduce 
dependency on other countries, especially China for unhindered availability of 
raw materials used in batteries. 
(Para 82) 
 
29. The Committee also recommends that Government should ensure 
strengthening supply chain network, e asy avai lability and accessibility to raw 
material and components for batteries, to promote EV adoption. 
(Para 83) 
 
30. The Committee notes that c urrently, loans for Internal Combustion 
Engine (ICE) vehicles are relatively easy to get with lower interest rates as the 
vehicle’s value is well -understood, making loans secure for the bank. However, 
this is not the case with EVs, as their residual value is not clear. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should designate EV as a 
priority lending sector, e specially financing for commercial fleets, as they are 
critical to the transition towards cleaner mobility. Availability of easy loans 
with lower interest and longer tenures will make it easier for the consumer to 

46 
 
go for EVs, which ultimately lead  to faster adoption of electric mobility across 
the country.   
(Para 82) 
 
31. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government and all other 
stakeholders (especially manufacturers) should make use of every feasible 
promotional and advertising platform to highli ght the benefits of Electric 
Vehicles and EV technology. Informational campaigns across print and 
electronic media can make a huge impact. In addition to the obvious benefits 
such as anti -pollution and cost -efficiency, busting myths such as battery 
longevity that surround EV usage may also be highlighted. Return on 
Investment (RoI) and cost of ownership benefits of EVs vis a vis conventional 
Internal Combustion Engines (ICE) can be demonstrated. Customers may also 
be educated about the various benefit s, incentives and subsidies offered by the 
Government such as exemptions of EVs from road tax during vehicle 
registration, discounts offered on purchase of EVs etc. 
(Para 87) 
 
32. The Committee observes that there is no sufficient R&D Support by the 
Ministry for  technological advancement. The spending in India on R&D is 
point less than 1 percent whereas  the major economies spend around 5 to 6 
percent.  Because of poor funding, India is lagging behind in R&D.  Without 
sufficient R&D, technological improvements/adv ancement is not possible.   The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that R&D facilities should be improved and 
its funding should also be enhanced. The M inistry of Heavy Industries has 
centers/autonomous bodies like Automotive Research Association of India  
(ARAI) and National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project 
(NATRIP) for R&D of I nternal Combustion Engine (ICE)  Vehicles. The 
Committee recommends that MHI should set -up R&D Cent ers for supporting 
EVs also for technological advancement. 
(Para 89) 
 
33. During the course of discussion it was suggested that Ministry of Heavy 
Industries and EV Manufacturers should jointly work together to undertake 
R&D for furthering the cause of ' Make-In-India' so that in the coming years 
country can become self-reliant in manufacturing EV batteries and components 
indigenously. The Committee , therefore, recommends that M HI and EV 

47 
 
manufacturers should make concerted efforts for setting up of a robust R&D 
infrastructure to promote indigenous manufacturing to reduce import s and 
achieving self-reliance through technology improvements and advancements 
(R&D). 
(Para 90) 
 
34. The Committee further recommends that the Government should focus 
on creating local manufacturing ecosystem at global scale in order to lower the 
price of EV batteries, which will ultimately help  to create EV demand. The 
Government should also focus on global competitiveness of indigenous EV 
industry. However, the most important element is to develop local EV parts 
manufacturing eco-system that is at global scale & quality. 
 
35. At p resent, there is no Government S cheme for incentivizing the local 
manufacturing of EV components other than battery cells. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that Government may mull over bringing a scheme 
focused on localizatio n of other critical EV components as that would give a 
good boost to Electric Mobility in India. 
(Para 92) 
 
36. Some of the Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs)  informed the 
Committee that they made a great progress in localizing major components. 
However, few child parts are still imported from other co untries like China. 
The import  duties have been increased from 5% to 15% to encourage local 
manufactures. But due to non -production of some of the                                  
child-parts/components, the cost of Production ha s increased due to hike in 
import duties. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Import duty may 
be raised only i n a phased manner till such components are manufactured 
locally. 
(Para 94) 
 
37. The aggressive push by the Governme nt and EV manufacturers will 
certainly see a massive EV I ndustry setup in the coming years , including 
battery production, EV specific assembly lines as well as the charging 
infrastructure.  This would naturally lead to a huge demand of technically 
skilled workforce in the area, as several auto makers have already announced 
their upcoming EV plans in the country.  Meeting this demand will not be 

48 
 
possible without the cooperation of the training institutes in the country. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends th at EV -specific trainings/courses should 
be included into the curriculum of premier institutes like  IITs, Engineering 
Colleges etc. to ensure that there is no scarcity of skilled manpower for India n 
EV Industry. 
 
(Para 96) 
 
38. The Committee further recomme nds that skill and capability building 
measures and skills improvement of manpower in handling fire safety hazards 
in case of EVs should be ensured. Up -skilling of workshop manpower to handle 
servicing and repair of electric powertrain, connected features,  vehicle analytics 
etc. should be done expeditiously. 
(Para 97) 
 
39. The Committee has been informed that at present EV Cars are taxed at 
5%, and big Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs) are taxed at 43% (28% GST plus 
15% Cess). EVs reduce energy consumption by  75% over Internal Combustion 
Engine (ICE)  while HEVs reduce energy consumption by 30 -45% over ICE 
without any external charger. Hence , HEVs are also entitled for discount on 
GST rate as in the case of EVs. GST sup port of HEV would help the whole       
eco-systems and provide impetus to EVs. The Committee , therefore, 
recommends that the GST rates on HEV may also be at a lower rate to create a 
lucrative EV ecosystem. 
 
(Para 100) 
40. The Committee observes that the intervention by the Government for 
promoting EV adoption by way of subsidies, financial support, R&D etc. in 
India is very minimal compared to other countries , which is the reason why the 
offtake of EV adoption in India has been very low.  The Committee desires that 
the Government should have focuse d strategy for enhancing its involvement for 
supporting the EV transition. 
(Para 102) 
 
41. The objective of the Government for adoption of Electric & Hybrid 
Mobility is to achieve reduction in fossil fuel consumption, pollution and 
Carbon Emission, reducin g net imports, realizing energy security, enhancing 
local manufacturing, creation of jobs etc. The Automobile Industry as a whole, 
even before the onset of Covid -19 Pandemic was going through slowdown due 

49 
 
to poor demand because of non -availability of finance to consumers. Moreover, 
the automobile and auto components manufacturers had made huge 
investments for the transition from BS -IV to BS -VI emission norms w.e.f.        
1st April, 2020. The Covid -19 Pandemic has further stalled the Auto Industry. 
Hence, given the prevailing precarious situation in the automobile sector, the 
Committee feels that to achieve the end objective, a  technology neutral 
approach to the EV Mobility would be prudent to ensure de -risking from the 
rapid technology transformations. 
(Para 109 (i)) 
 
42. The Committee has also been informed that technology innovations are 
occurring rapidly and other options i.e. Hydrogen and alternate fuels such as 
Ethanol are also coming up.  Therefore, the committee is of the view that 
widening the techno logy options would be a better approach in the journey 
ahead.  Further, Government policy support may be provided to all electrified 
technologies (BEV, HEV, PHEV & FCEV) , which will ensure a disruption free 
and faster transition from ICE vehicles. 
(Para 109 (ii)) 
 
43. The Committee is hopeful that with the trend of fall in battery prices and  
indigenous production of batteries and EV Components, the gap between the 
price of EV in comparison with similar I nternal Combustion Engine (ICE)  
model/category will be  bridged soon and the consumers will shift to e -mobility 
given its low total cost of ownership.  The Committee further hopes that 
measures such as creation of demand for local manufacturing, reduction in 
GST rate for Hybrid EVs, announcements of long -term policy measures for 
Electric and Hybrid Vehicles, provision of subsidy for EVs, revisiting PLI 
Scheme, incentive for scrapping of ICE vehicles while purchasing EVs, 
availability of easy and affordable financing options for EV components, 
inclusion  of EVs in Priority Sector Lending, extension of subsidy under 
FAME-II scheme to e3Ws and private e4Ws, enhancing awareness among 
people about EV adoption, extension of Government support for Research & 
Development in the field of EV manufacture, robust EV chargin g 
infrastructure etc. would accelerate the EV penetration in transport sector, as 
per the targets set by the Government. 
 
(Para 109 (iii))

THIRTY-FIRST REPORT OF THE COMMiTTEE 
I. the Chairman, Department -related Parliamentary Standing Comm ittee on Industry having been 
authorised by the Committee to present the Repon on its behalf, present this Thiny-first Repon of the 
Commiuee on the Demands for Grants of the Department of Mines for 1999-2000. 
While examining the sa id Demands for Grants. the Commiuee also considered the Action Taken 
Notes of Dcp~nment of Mines on its 24th Repon penaining to the Demands for Grants of Department of 
Mme~ for 1998-99. Tite Commineeexamined the relevan t docume nts and papers relating to the Demands 
for Gra nts for 1999-2000 received from the Department of Mines. It also heard the oral evidence of 
Secretary. Depanment of Mtnes on the budgetary provisions as contained m the detailed o.;mands for 
Grants. 
The Committee adopted the Repon in its meeting held on the 16th April, 1999. 
The comments and observations with suitable recommendation~ of the Committee are given in the 
succeeding paragraphs : 
I. Gcologtcal Survey of India is a premier organisatton under the umbrella of Department of Mines. 
It goes without saying that ever since its inception. it has made immense contribution to the growth and 
development of mining sector of the economy. The servtces of Geological Survey of India in the field of 
geological surveying and mapping have helped the nation in the exploration and the exploitation pf the 
mineral re~ources. The vast tract of the minerals would h3vc remained unutilised but for the untiring 
endeavour of GSI to locate more mincrnl-rich areas. The Dcpanmcnt Related Parliamentary Standing 
Commiuec on lnduMry has, time and again, appn.>ciated the efTons of the Geological Survey of India and 
once again .tpplauds the unflagging commitment of the technocrat s of this organisation to the goal of 
optimum ham<.:ssing of mineral resources of the country. Thi~ is precisely the reason why this Commiuee 
has been advocating for higher budgetary allocations for it. It ha.~ been the considered view of the Commiuee 
that orgamsatio ns hke GSI must not be allowed to feel th" pmch of the cash swrved economy of India. As 
the efforts of >uch organisations have done yeoman's service to the well being of millions of Indians. The 
Commiuec also lauds the effons of Depanment of Mines in pursuing the case of GSI with as much zeal 
a> 11 had expected it to do. As a result of this, the budgetary allocation earmarked for GSI has registered 
an upsw ing over the years. This in turn. has allnwcd GSI to function without any major financial 
unpcdiment> . It augurs well for this core sector of the economy. 
Yet. there are <1 coup le of other problems which are staring at GSI as it looks forward to enter the 
next millennium. TI1e nineues of the 20th century witnessed major policy upheaval s on the econom•c 
front in India . At a time the buuword m world economies both capitalist and socialist, was to mtegratc 
with the new emergmg world order, India could not have afforded to isolate itself from the main$tream. 
This urge to integrate with the world economy sowed the seeds of economic liberalisation in India. The 
prO<:ess of hberalisauon brought the crucial element of competition mto the mind>et of lndtan entrepreneurs 
and the organisatio ns engaged in the promotion of ovemll industrial growth. Being one among them, the 
Geologica l Survey of India, although. h;t~ kept pace with the changing times yet it needs to equip itself 
with the latc't state of the an technology in order to sustrun the tempo of its endeavours. The Commiuee 
ha~ taken a very sympathetic view of the obsolescence of the equtpments being used by the GSI. Its age· 
old ship has also failed to keep strides with the needs of a comple tely changed economic and industrial 
scenario. lienee, the modernisation of Geological Survey of India. 

2 
The Committee, the~rore, recommends the setting up or an expert panel to look into all the· 
aspects or modernisation Including the aerial prospecting system of the Geological Survey of India 
and to prepare a comprehensive action plan along with its financial implications. The Committee 
also recommends that the modalities of the expert panel should be as comprehensive as possible so 
os to include all the aspects of modernisation. Also, the expert panel should have a definite deadline 
for submitting its report within the current rmancial year in order to avoid any kind of delay as it 
would totally defeat the very purpose behind the setting up of the panel. 
As regards the replacement of GSI's ship, the Committee is of the opinion that till such time 
a decision is taken to purchase a new ship for it, the Department of Mines maY. allow GSI to take a 
~hip on lease from the Department or Ocean. 
2. With the announcement of the New Mineral Policy. the doors of mining sector were opened for 
the private and foreign investment. The aim behtnd liberal norms as envisaged in the New Mineral Policy 
was to bring in more area.~ into prospecting and mining of precious metals and minerals. Industrialisation 
of backward areas as a result of the exploitation of available natural resources was also one of the intended 
purposes. The flow of foreign investment in this sector was also expected to make enough funds available 
for being diverted to the social sector. However, given the figures of the outgoing financial year, the 
picture of foreign direct investment is not as rosy as the policy makers of the country might have envisioned . 
According to the Secretary. Department of Mines the actual inflow of foreign investment in mining sector 
in the year 1998-99 is only Rs. 80 crore ;u against the approvals of Rs. 3300 crore. This glaring wedge 
between the actual inflow and the approvals of FDJ proposals bears a testimony to the existing state of . ,, 
affairs on this front. Since, the approval of the concerned State Government is must before a project gets 
the green signal, it is alleged that the proposals get stuck in the Secretariats of the State Governments. 
Hence, the delay in the clearance of the projects. Therefore. the State Governments are, primarily. 
responsible for the targeted FDI flow not fructifying. 
But in the view of the Committee, it would be totally unjustifiable to hold the State Government 
alone, responsible for the delay in the clearance of the mining projects. The Union Government cannot 
exonerate itself by blaming the State Governments. Rather, it should stnve hard to see that the proJeCL~ 
are cleared in time. Anyway, it is not the intention of this Comm1nee to act as an arbiter between the two. 
What, however, needs the observation of this Committee is the absence of an effective mechanism to 
precipitate speedy and timely clearance of FDI propos;! IS at all stages and levels. 
With this view in mind, the Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should 
constitute a high powered authority on the lines of the propO$cd "Foreign Investment Implementation 
Authority" to ensure that the actual inflow of foreign investment does not lag behind the total 
approvals. Such an authority should have the representation of the concerned State Governments 
as its full time members in order to see that the hurdles in the way of on FDI proposal are removed 
forthwith. Once a mechanism like this, the Committee hopes, is put into place, it would go a long 
way in not only improving the credibility of the country among the foreign investors but would al~o 
help the mining sector grow manifold. 
3. Public Sector Undertakings, from time to time embark upon modernisation and expansion of 
their existing manufacturing equipment and capacities . Likewise PSUs under the administrative control 
of Depanment of Mines, namely, NALCO, BALCO, HZL and HCL are implementing or going to 
implement modernisation and expansion programmes in their various production units. like the expansion 
of BALCO's Bauxite Mine and Alumina Refinery Complex and Smelter & Captive Power Plant, 
modernisation of BALCO's Alumma Plant at Korba, Aluminium Smelter at Korba. Cast llouse Unit, 
Steam Generation Plant and Conductor & Foil Plant (BBU) and expansion of its Captive Power Plant. 
expansion of HZL's Zinc Smelter, modernisation of concentrator plants of Hindustan Copper Ltd. at 
• 

3 
Indian Copper Complex, Khetri Copper Complex and Malanjkhand Copper Project and expans ion of 
smelter and PMR Plam (Refinery) of Indian Copper Complex, Khetri. 
All these modernisation and expansio n programmes involved a hefty outgo of financial resources of 
these companies . If these programmes are not striclly implemented within t11e prescribed deadlines, there 
arises a situation whereby, they run imo cost and time over-runs. The point, the Commictcc wishes to 
make is that it is quite worrisome and disturbing that PSUs have a common history of not being able to 
implement ~uch programmes within the time and cost limits. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department of Mines, in consultation with 
the Management of the PSUs under its administrative jurisdiction, should con~titutc a Special 
Ta_~k Force to oversee the implementation of modernisation and expansion programm es of these 
!'SUs in order to avoid cost and time over-runs. The Committee, also recommends that accountability 
should be fixed and appropriate punitive action is taken , if any over-runs are detected. 
4. The Government is going to divest its majority stake in BALCO. A global advisor called M/s 
Jardine Fleming has also been engaged for this purpose. The Commictee would like to draw the allcntion 
of Department of Mines to the allegations often, levelled against certain Public Sector Undertakings 
wherein their shares were, clandc$tinely, offered at much less a price than their actual market value. in the 
name of disinvestment. Transparency, in the whole e~ereise, was also not maintained. 
This is why, the Committee is of the considered view that Department of Mines should see to 
it thnt the disinvestment programme of BALCO is closely monitored, transparency is maintained 
and the real value of the equity shares i.s realised. In thl~ whole process, the interests of tbe workers 
of BALCO should not only be kept in mind but be pr otected also. 
5. Hindustan Copper Ltd. has been incurring losses over the years due to a host of factors. In order 
that this PSU regain its viability. the Government has sanctioned Rs. 414 crore for its restructuring plan 
to be implemented in the next couple of years. It is the considered view of the Committee that the health 
of PSUs. in general. is prone to sickness owing to a variety of reasons. Their health being so susceptible 
to the onslaughts of the market forces, it becomes even more vital that they are not allowed to slip into the 
morass of siclmess. Forthis, managerial dexterity and acumen should be the order of the day if a PSU bas 
to survive the vagaries of the fast changing economic and industrial scenario. The country, already short 
of adequate financial resources, cannot afford to pump crorcs of rupees into the PSUs at the expense of 
other social obligations. 
It is, therefore, recommended that both the Department of Mines as well as the Management 
of Hindustan Copper Ltd. should ensure proper implementation of the restructuring plan of the 
company in order to see that it bears the desired fruitful results. The Committee also recommends 
that funds earmarked as per the sanct ioned package a.re made timely available to HCL and it 
· ~hould be ensured that the funds are spent within a specified timeframe. 
6. Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. is another PSU of Department of Mines which has been 
pas~ing throug h difficult times. The Committee was informed that the recommendations of the Expert 
Committee set up for the revival of MECL. are being implemented. As a result, it ha.~ been possible to 
reduce the losses of the Corporation in 1998-99. Still, tlte excess manpower of this PSU is proving to be 
a major hurdle in its efforts to become viable. Around 700 workers need to be separated. With this aim in 
mind, a sum of Rs. 3.45 crore i~ proposed to be spent from the central pool of a new scheme or Grants-in­
aid for implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme by the PSUs in the year 1999-2000. The amount 
of Rs. 3.45 crore is too meagre to fully shed the surplus manpower. Interestingly, Hindustan Copper Ltd. 
777 RS F-3·A 

4 
has bee n allocated Rs. 100 crore for 1999·2000 for the rational isation of its manpower, of course, from 
the overall package of Rs. 414 crore meant for its capi tal restructuring which inter-olio involves separation 
of 11000 surplus workers. The Commiuee fails to comprehend the reason as to why 700 workers cannot 
be scpanued at one go by making adequate budgetary provision for the purpose and that too keeping in 
mind the precarious condition of MECL. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. should be 
provided with sufficient funds to enable It to separate its surplus manpower either from the pool of 
Grants-in-aid scheme or any other bud getary source without any further dela y. 
7. The Committee is deeply anguished and concerned at the sorry state of affairs prevailing in 
Bhar.1t Gold Mines Ltd. In the absence of a clear-cut policy on the pan of the Government, the fate ofthi~ 
PSU contin ues to hang in balance for long. This apparent dithering on the part of the Government has 
resu lted in the accentuation of the clouds of uncert.ainty ove r BGML . The direct victims of this 
indecisiveness are the workers of BGML. The long pending case before BIFR has also added to the woes 
of the workers. 
According to the candid submission of Secretary, Depanment of Mines before the Com mittee, the 
cost of opemtions in the gold mines is too high as a result ofwhtch the whole production is unviable. The 
idea of fmding a joint venture panner ha.~ also been broached . It appears that the Government might be 
totking the final dec ision in respect of Bharnt Gold Mines Ltd. 
The Committee is oft he view that while taking :any final decision on the future of Bharat Gold 
M incs Ltd., the Government should adopt a sympat heti c approach towards the workers. A generous 
VRS package ror the workers could be a way out to mitigate the hardships of the workers . 
8. While examining the Demands for Grants ofDepanmen t of Mines for 1999-2000, the Committee 
was informed that the Departmen t has set up a 'Mi neral Exploration Fund' with a view to lessen the 
dependence ofMineral Explomtio n Corporation Ltd. on budget support. This fund will receive contributions 
from profit maki ng PSUs of Departmen t of Mines. namely NALCO, BALCO and HZL at the rateof20 % 
pertonne of crude reso urces ofthe mineral being explo ited by them. The fund, at present, has a corpu s of 
Rs. 6.2 crore. 
The Committee appreciat es the crution of ' Mineral Exploration Fund' and hopes that it will 
prove to be a shot in the ann of the Mineral Explo rati on Corporation Ltd. and wiU go a long way 
in meeting the need ror financial resourc es in the rield of expl oration activiti es. At the same time, 
the Comm itte e would also Uke to recomm end that the Department of Mines should also explore the 
feos ibiUty of involving Jlrivate sector companies for contributing to this Fund like the private 
sec tor steel company TIS CO makes contri butions to the 'Steel Development Fund'. Ln the opinion 
of the Committee , contributions from both publi c as well as private sector companies to the Fund 
would be in the overall interest of the mining sector. 
9. Sikkim Minmg Corporation is another loss making PSU under the administrative jurisdiction of 
Department of Mines. It is also in dire straits. It has been recurring constant losses. The Department of 
Mines in its Action Taken Repon on the recommen dation pertaining to Sikkim Minmg Corporat ion as 
con tained in the 24th Report of the Commi uce on Demand s for Grants of Department of Mines for 1998-
99, has stated that the Sikkim Mining Corporat ion has plans to pursue a number of expansion and 
diversificat ion schemes to make the Corpomtion flexible and more viable. 
With the budgetary provision of mere Rs. 38 lakh for 1999-2000 and no proposal to raise IEBR, the 
Committee wonders ns to how this PSU is going to pursue its planned expansion and dive rsification 
schemes. 

5 
The Committee, therefore, is or the view that the Department of Mines should come up with a

REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises on the recommendations  contained in the 
Committee’s 304th Report on the Demands for Grants (2021-22) pertaining to M/o MSME. 
 
2.  Action Taken Note have  been received from the Ministry of Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises  in respect of the recommendations /observations contained in the          
304th Report. These have been categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter-I-       The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry 
  Para:  28, 37, 53, 61, 73, 74, 83, 85, 86, 87, 88 and 103 (Total: 12) 
 
Chapter-II-  The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to   
pursue further in view of the Ministry’s replies. 
Para: 11, 12, 15, 17, 25, 31, 41, 43, 56, 62, 69, 70, 90 and 104 (Total: 14) 
 
Chapter-III-  The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not 
accepted replies of the Ministry.  
  Para: 3, 4, 13, 23, 24, 38, 39, 42, 48, 49, 54, 63, 65, 78, 79 and 84  
(Total: 16) 
 
Chapter-IV- Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Ministry are still awaited.  
Para: 55  (Total: 01) 
 
3. The details of the Action Taken Replies of the Ministry and further recommendations/ 
observations of the Committee thereon wherever found necessary are given in the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
 
Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1. The Committee appreciates the effort made by the Ministry in respect of 
creating e -market linkages for strengthening the MSME Sector and recommends 
that the Ministry should analyze the marketing system of MSMEs of developed 
countries and their system of ne wer technology adoption for their development 
and adopt the best practices followed internationally for advancement and 
development of indigenous MSMEs.  
 
(Para 28) 
 
Action Taken 
 
The Procurement and Marketing Support Scheme provides market support 
to MSMEs by promoting new market access initiatives like 
organising/participation in Trade Fairs/Exhibitions, Vendor Development 
Programmes etc. with in the country. The International Cooperation (IC) Scheme 
provides financial supp ort to the MSME sector for participating in international 
exhibitions/fairs to exhibit their products.  The recommendation of Committee has 
been noted for further necessary action. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
2. PMEGP is one of the flagship Schemes of the  Ministry of MSME which is 
capable of generating large -scale employment for youth of the country, 
particularly during the Covid Pandemic. The Committee , however, finds that an 
amount Rs. 2000 crore has been allocated for the Scheme for FY 2021-2022 vis-à-
vis allocation of Rs. 2500 crores during 2020 -2021. The Committee recommends 
that more allocations should be demanded by the Ministry at the RE stage for 
effective implementation of the Scheme. 
(Para 37) 
Action Taken 
 
An amount of Rs.1905.80 crores (Margin Money of Rs.1877.33 crores+ 
Backward & Forward Linkages of Rs.28.47 crores) was allocated under the 
PMEGP Scheme for the year 2020 -21 at Revised Estimates (RE) stage. In 
addition, an unspent balance of Rs. 499.28 crore as on 1 st April, 2020 was also 
available. During the FY 2020 -21, PMEGP has performed very well and achieved 
its annual targets by assisting 74,415 applicants in setting up new microenterprises 

 
 
3 
 
through disbursing a subsidy of Rs. 2,188 crores and generating employment 
opportunities for an estimated 5.7 lakh persons.   
 
Banks during 2020 -21 have sanctioned about one lakh applications, which 
are 50% more over the last year. Approval rate of the applications forwarded to 
the banks also increased from 21.6% in 2019 -20 to 25.6% in 2020 -21. This has 
been PMEGP’s best performance since its inception in 2008 -09 despite COVID 
challenges throughout the year.  
 
For the FY 2021 -22 (Budget Estimate) an amount of Rs. 2000.00 crores 
(MM of Rs.1900 crores + B&F 100.00 crores) have been allocated. However, a 
target for setting up of at least one lakh new units under PMEGP for the year 
2021-22 has been fixed. The additional budget requirement will accordingly be 
requested in due course through Supplementary Grants.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3. The Committee notes that the BE for SFURTI Scheme for FY 2020 -21 i.e. 
Rs. 464.85 crore was reduced at the RE Stage to Rs. 300 crore and the Actual 
Expenditure was only Rs. 192.54 crores till 31 st January, 2021. The Committee 
also notes that against a projected Budget Estimate of Rs. 500 crores for the 
SFRUTI Scheme for FY 2021-2022, an allocation of only Rs. 170 crores has been 
made. The Committee expresses its concern over the low utilization pat tern and 
reduction in allocations for an important Scheme of the Ministry, which is capable 
of generating employment in a large scale in the rural areas for the artisans, 
particularly during the Covid Pandemic. The Committee recommends that a 
holistic evaluation study of the Scheme may be conducted and based on the said 
study more allocations should be projected by the Ministry at the RE Stage for 
effective implementation of SFURTI Scheme for benefit of the traditional artisans. 
 
(Para 53) 
 
Action Taken 
 
The RE for the year 2020 -21 was Rs. 350 crores out of which Rs.349.110 
cores was utilized which is 99.74% of the RE. For FY 2021 -2022, more funds 
shall be sought at RE stage based on the progress to implement the Scheme.  An 
evaluation study of the Scheme has been under taken by IIM Lucknow.  Based on 
the report and internal assessment, the Scheme shall be carried forward with 
required changes for the benefit of the traditional artisans across the country.  

 
 
4 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4. The Committee observes that one of the most important objectives of the 
implementation of various Schemes under Coir Board is the creation of 
employment especially in rural areas of the country. For this purpose, Coir Board 
is providing training on various  aspects of production and development of 
new/innovative products. The Committee recommends that Ministry should make 
these training courses popular through various social publicity mediums available 
so that large number of people especially from younger g eneration may get 
attracted to such training courses, which will culminate in fruitful employment. 
 
(Para 61) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Presently, the Coir Board through its Regional /Sub Regional Offices is 
making efforts to  popularize its training courses through the concerned District 
Industries Centers, Directorate of Industries, Coir Project Offices,  SHGs, NGOs, 
various co -operative societies etc. Further, through the conduct of promotional 
programs viz. Entrepreneurship Development Programme, Awareness 
Programme, Workshops, seminars etc., more people including the younger 
generation are being made aware about coir training courses.  On the website of 
the Board, videos and e-tutorials on various coir processing and applications have 
been uploaded. During the year 2020 -21, 29 National/ Regional level webinars on 
various topics on coir and Schemes and services were conducted which were 
attended virtually by more th an 35,000 participants/ viewers including from other 
social media like WhatsApp groups, Face book, You Tube etc. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
5. During the lockdown periods the availability of raw material was disrupted 
which affected the operations of MSMEs adversely. Further, the prices of raw 
material have risen exorbitantly in the recent times which have significantly 
affected the businesses of  the MSMEs and their profits have significantly 
decreased. In this given scenario, NSIC can play a significant role by 
coordinating with the respective Ministries to ensure unhindered supply of raw 
material to MSMEs and also provided support and interventi ons to the MSMEs in 
the export of their products. The Committee expresses its satisfaction that NSIC 
performed well since II Quarter and facilitated the MSMEs to the tune of Rs. 
1234.91 crores. The Committee is however, of the view that the Ministry should  

 
 
5 
 
also explore other possibilities for raw material supply to MSMEs instead of 
solely depending on NSIC to meet the raw material requirements of MSMEs . 
 
 
(Para 73) 
 
6. The Committee recommends that a robust procurement system should be 
evolved which could ensure unhindered and timely supply of raw materials to 
MSMEs at reasonable price. The Committee recommends that required steps 
should be taken to keep the prices of ra w material reasonable, including giving 
some sort of subsidy, so that MSMEs can run their businesses smoothly.  
 
(Para 74) 
 
Action Taken (For Para 73 and 74) 
 
To ensure regular supply of raw material to MSMEs, National Small 
Industries Corporation (NSIC), a CPSE under this Ministry , facilitates MSMEs in 
meeting their raw material requirements. For this purpose, NSIC enters into 
arrangements with bulk manufacturers for supply of raw materials to MSMEs. 
NSIC also provides financial assistance to MSMEs under i ts Raw Material 
Assistance Scheme against bank guarantee for payment to suppliers. 
 
Further, Government of India has taken various steps to ensure continuous 
supply of raw materials to MSMEs. Some of the steps taken to meet the raw 
material demands of MSMEs in the Steel Sector are as under:  
 Guidelines have been issued on 24.06.2020 by Ministry of Steel for 
providing limited quantum of four product categories of steel (hot rolled 
coil, cold rolled coil, wire rods and alloy steel bars) to MSME members of 
Engineering Export Promotion Council (EEPC) at export parity price by 
domestic producers.  
 Relief has also been provided to metal recyclers by exempting Basic 
Customs Duty (BCD) on steel scrap and reducing BCD to 2.5% on copper 
scrap as well as revocation/temporary revocation of ADD and CVD on 
certain steel products.  
 Besides, production of iron  ore and steel by mining companies and major 
steel producers has been increased to ensure steady availability of steel for 
use by MSMEs. 
 
 

 
 
6 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
7. The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development 
Programmes sensitize and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST enterprises, to 
become qualified vendors to public sector enterprises and other Government 
Departments as per the provision of 25% mandatory procurement under Public 
Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from SC/ST MSEs. However, during 
its visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020, the Committee 
found that while the PSUs and Government procurement from MSEs has been 
gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST units is negligible. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that there should be more Vendor Development 
Programmes organized to popularize Public Procurement Policy among MSEs 
especially SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs. 
(Para 83) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Under National SC -ST Hub, Special Vendor Development Progr ams 
(SVDPs) are organized through NSSH Offices in coordination with 
CPSEs/Central Ministries and local industry associations to encourage the SC/ST 
enterprises to be part of public procurement. Post such outreach activities, training 
in e-tendering and handholding support for participation in Govt. Tenders are also 
provided to interested SC -ST entrepreneurs through the National SC -ST Hub 
offices located at various places. Since its inception, 335SVDPs have been 
organized under the NSSH. In addition, more th an 1500SVDPs have been 
conducted in collaboration with CPSEs and various Industry Associations.  
 
Since the inception of the NSSH, there has been a 10-fold growth in the public 
procurement from SC/ST MSEs. The procurement made from SC/ST MSEs from 
FY 2015-16 to FY 2020-21 are as under:

However, the recommendation of the Committee has been noted.  
 

 
 
7 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
8. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual 
Expenditure has always been less than the BE. The Committee is concerned about 
the under-utilization of allocated funds meant for the marginalized communities of 
the society. The Committee recommends that Ministry should endeavor to improve 
the situation by ensuring that the budget earmarked for SC/ST Hub Scheme is 
utilized fully for the benefit of the communities. Creating awareness among SC/ST 
entrepreneurs, ground level support and handhold ing of SC/ST entrepreneurs may 
work well in improving the performance of this Scheme. Underutilization of funds 
is a serious cause of concern for the Committee; therefore, Ministry is advised to 
ensure full utilization of funds. 
(Para 85)

The Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme: 
a) ISEC Scheme was introduced in May 1977 to mobilize funds from the 
banking institutions to fill the gaps in the actual fund requirement and 
availability from budgetary sources. 
b) The Scheme is applicable for all registered Khadi Institutions/Coop 
Societies/Trusts under KVIC/KVIB. 
c) The Khadi Institutions shall pay 4% interest and the difference between 
the actual lending rate of interest minus 4% which will be borne by KVIC. 
d) ISEC limit is fixed for the Khadi Institutions based on their level of 
production and/or sales and the estimated requirement of funds in 
accordance with the prescribed pattern of assistance of KVIC to meet the 
working capital requirement.   
Reasons f or non -availment of 100% of ISEC issued by KVIC by Khadi 
Institutions: 
 
i. KVIC and banks were following different methods of assessing the 
working capital requirements of the KIs.  
ii. KVIC is assessing the Working Capital based on the target fixed on 
Production, Retail Sales, Wholesales, Vastragar, Raw Material and 
processing only, whereas, the banks are considering available opening 
inventory level of finished goods and credit facilities being extended by 
the trade creditors also. 
iii. Besides RBI guidelines each ba nk has issued internal guidelines also for 
the assessment of working capital based on the turn over with the 
institution’s contribution. 
iv. The recycling of working capital (i.e., operating cycle) is being assessed 
@ 16 months by KVIC, whereas the banks are c alculating at a maximum 
of 4 months as applicable for other Textile Industries.  
v. Bankers are mostly considering fixing the C.C. limit @ 20% on the total 
turnover of the Khadi Institutions as that of extending loan facilities to the 
private/commercial establishments. 
vi. Bankers are expecting to realize sundry debtor’s dues by 90 days.  

 
 
12 
 
vii. Bankers are insisting to maintain 130% stock on hand  on the C.C.   
limit fixed by them. 
viii.     The banks are also insisting on collateral security for some cases and   
failure to furnish by the KIs also results in lesser availment. 
 
Due to the above reasons, bankers are not coming forward for extending the 
credit facilities by honouring the ISEC issued by KVIC in general and NER in 
particular. 
 
However, the matter is being examined  in the Ministry to relook at the 
present methodology for estimation of ISEC value for Khadi Institutions. There 
must be uniformity between the methodology used by KVIC to issue ISEC 
certificate and the working capital calculation methodology adopted by ba nks, to 
reduce the gap between ISEC being certified by KVIC and working capital 
amount sanctioned by banks. 
 
With a view to creating greater awareness among the bankers, KVIC is 
taking up the core subject matter in the SLBC meetings.

The Guarantee Emergency Credit Line (GECL) Scheme is implemented by 
the National Credit Guarantee Trust Company , which is under the administrative 
control of the Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance. The  
Ministry of  MSME is thus releasin g the funds for the corpus created for 
extending guarantees under this Scheme on the advice of the Department of  
Financial Services. The Scheme was earlier being implemented as the Emergency 
Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) by the Department of Financial Services. 
 
The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) was announced as 
part of the AatmaNirbhar Bharat Package in 2020 with the objective to help 
MSMEs/small businesses to meet their operational liabilities and resume 
businesses in view of the distress caused by the COVID -19 crisis, by providing 
member lending institutions (MLIs) 100 percent guarantee against any losses 
suffered by them due to non -repayment of the ECLGS funding by borrowers. An 
overall ceiling of Rs. 3 lakh crores of guarantees was approved.  

 
 
30 
 
 
Since its launch, the ECLGS has undergone extensions and changes keeping 
in view of the impact of Covid on various sectors of the economy and the 
emerging needs. All these changes were made within the overall ceiling of the Rs. 
3 lakh crores guarantee cover.   In May 2021, on account of the disrupt ions caused 
by the second wave of the COVID 19 pandemic to businesses across various 
sectors of the economy, the Government has further enlarged the scope of ECLGS 
as under: 
i. Overall cap of admissible guarantee has been raised by Rs. 1.5 lakh crore - 
from 3 lakh crore to 4.5 lakh crore. 
ii. Launch of fourth component as ECLGS 4.0:  Provided 100% guarantee to 
MLIs for extending loans up to Rs. 2 crores to hospitals/nursing 
homes/clinics/medical colleges for setting up on -site oxygen generation 
plants. Interest rate under this is capped at 7.5%; 
iii. Extension in period of repayment to ECLGS borrowers who are eligible for 
restructuring as per RBI guidelines of 05.05.2021; 
iv. Additional ECLGS assistance  of up to 10% of the outstanding as on 
29.02.2020 to borrowers covered un der ECLGS 1.0, in tandem with 
restructuring as per RBI guidelines of 05.05.2021; 
v. Removal of ceiling of Rs. 500 crores of loan outstanding for eligibility under 
ECLGS 3.0  subject to maximum additional ECLGS assistance to each 
borrower being limited to 40% or Rs.200 crore, whichever is lower; 
vi. Civil Aviation sector  (scheduled and non -scheduled airlines, chartered flight 
operators, air ambulances and airports) made eligible under ECLGS 3.0;  
vii. Validity of ECLGS extended to 30.09.2021  or till guarantees for an amou nt 
of Rs. 4.5 lakh crore are issued 
The design of ECGLS provides flexibility to quickly respond to emerging 
needs, as has been evidenced by the introduction of ECLGS 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 as 
well as changes as mentioned above, all of which were within available  headroom 
of Rs . 3 lakh crores. Currently, about Rs. 2.73 lakh crores (2 -7-2021) of loans 
have been sanctioned under ECLGS. Keeping in view the changes announced in 
the Scheme recently, extension of limit of one time restructuring to Rs. 50 crores 
by RBI o n 04.06.2021 and the continuing adverse impact of COVID on 
businesses, it was decided to enhance the existing overall guarantee limit of Rs. 3 
lakh crores to Rs. 4.50 lakh crores. At 15% default estimation, the additional 
requirement of corpus is worked out at Rs. 22, 500 crores. 
 
As per the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC), loans 
amounting to Rs 2.73 lakh crores have been sanctioned till 02.07.2021 out of

Reasons for non -availment of 100% of the ISEC issued by KVIC by Khadi 
Institutions are as follows: 
 
i. KVIC and banks were following diff erent methods of assessing the 
working capital requirements of the KIs.  
ii. KVIC is assessing the Working Capital based on the target fixed on 
Production, Retail Sales, Wholesales, Vastragar, Raw Material and 
processing only, whereas, the banks are considering available opening 
inventory level of finished goods and credit facilities being extended by 
the trade creditors also. 
iii. Besides RBI guidelines each bank has issued internal guidelines also for 
the assessment of working capital based on the turn o ver with the 
institution’s contribution. 
iv. The recycling of working capital (i.e., operating cycle) is being assessed 
@ 16 months by KVIC, whereas the banks are calculating at a maximum 
of 4 months as applicable for other Textile Industries.  
v. Bankers are most ly considering fixing the C.C. limit @ 20% on the total 
turnover of the Khadi Institutions as that of extending loan facilities to the 
private/commercial establishments. 
vi. Bankers are expecting to realize sundry debtor’s dues by 90 days.  
vii. Bankers are insistin g to maintain 130% stock on hand for the C.C. 
limit fixed by them. 
viii. The banks are also insisting on collateral security for some cases and 
failure to furnish this by the KIs also results in lesser availment.

KVIC in general and NEZ in particular.

amount sanctioned by banks.

uniformity between the methodology used by KVIC to issue ISEC certificate 
and the working capital calculation methodology adopted by banks  for 
bridging the gaps between ISEC being certified by KVIC and working 
capital amount sanctioned by banks. 

 
 
40 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
37. The Committee is constrained to note that out of 371 clusters which have 
been approved, only 82 clusters are operational so far. The Commi ttee 
recommends that the process of setting up of SFURTI clusters should be 
expedited; targets should be set and ensure that the approved clusters are 
completed and become operational within the stipulated timeframe for benefit of 
artisans.   
(Para 54) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
The implementation period of the projects envisaged under the Scheme in 
2014-15 and at the time of continuation of the Scheme in 2017 -18 was 3 years.  
This time period was revised to 12 -18 months in March 2020.  As on 30.4.2021, 
145 projects have become operational out of 401 approved which is about 36% of 
projects.  This is an improvement of 14% over earlier report (82/371 i.e. , 22% 
operational clusters).  With the reduced timelines, it is expected that more and 
more clusters shall become functional in the current year.  
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee is deeply concerned at the slow pace of 
operationalization of the SFURTI projects.  Normally, t he time taken from 
approval of the projects to the operationalization of the projects takes very 
long time, which adversely affects the whole Scheme and potential artisans  
and rural entrepreneurs . The Committee , therefore,  recommends that 
concrete and result -oriented steps should be taken by the Ministry to 
expedite the whole process of operationalization of SFURTI clusters/projects 
by removing all the hindrances such as pr ocedural delays , insufficiency of 
funds etc. for ensuring timely operationalization of the SFURTI projects. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
 
38. The Committee observes that the Skill Development Programmes  organised 
especially in respect of the ‘Physically Handicapped’ Category is not up to the 
mark. The Committee accordingly recommends that more Skill Development 
Programmes may be organized among various categories of people for improving 

 
 
41 
 
their skills for gainful employment in the coir sector. Online training sessions may 
also be organized as per feasibility and practicality. 
(Para 63) 
 
Action Taken 
 
The Coir Board is implementing skill development programmes for all categories 
of people including handicappe d artisans.  The videos and e -tutorials uploaded on 
the Board’s website can also be used by physically handicapped aspirants for 
getting online training on various coir technologies and processing and further 
starting self-employment. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee would like to be apprised of the number of Skill 
Development Programmes, number of persons  benefitted and the amount 
spent on these programmes. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
39. The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs. 100 crore was made in BE 
for Solar Charkha Mission for FY 2020 -21 but at the RE Stage , it got only Rs. 
0.04 crore. Further, for FY 2021 -22, an allocation of Rs. 5.04 crore has been 
made at BE Stage. The Committee recommends that more budgetary allocations 
should be made for such a good and eco -friendly Scheme capable of providing 
employment in rural areas and accordingly, the Ministry should project for more 
allocations at RE Stage for setting up of more Solar Charkha Clusters across the 
country. Besides, t he Ministry should provide timely interventions so that the 
Solar Charkha Clusters so set up are operationalized in an expeditious manner.  
 
(Para 65) 
 
Action Taken 
 
As part of the Scheme, 9 Promoter Agencies (PAs) were selected and they 
are yet to start the projects due to various reasons/challenges. The Scheme did not 
get a response on the expected lines. In view of this, and as per the advice of NITI 
Ayog and Ministry of Finance, the Scheme will be further taken up for 
extension/as new proposal based on the learnings of the already approved projects.  
 
 

 
 
42 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee would like to be intimated about the progress in the 
matter.  As already suggested, mor e funds may be sought at RE stage so that 
Solar Cha rkha clusters can be set up across the length and breadth of the 
country, thereby generating employment to the rural population.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
40. The Committee desired that delay in payments by CPSEs and Government 
Departments affects MSMEs adversely as they need cash flow to run their 
businesses. The Committee however, recommends that delayed payments of 
MSMEs from CPSEs be monitored through the SA MBANDH and SAMADHAAN 
Portals regularly and the pending payments of MSMEs may be cleared by CPSEs 
and other Government agencies at the earliest for strengthening the liquidity of 
MSMEs. 
(Para 78) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 With the Announcement of the package under A tmaNirbhar Bharat, a 
special sub -portal within SAMADHAAN has been created to track the delayed 
payment to the MSMEs from the CPSEs. 
 
Further, in case the process of resolution of grievances raised on 
SAMADHAN portal is taking time or no resolution is being  provided, provisions  
have been made under the CHAMPIONS portal to register grievances about non 
resolution of issues/grievances raised through the SAMADHAN portal.    
 
The Committee would like to be apprised of the grievances redressed 
though SAMADHAN por tal and CHAMPIONS portal respectively and the 
reasons for non -redressed of grievances even after the registration is done on 
CHAMPIONS portal. 
 
The Committee further impressed upon the Ministry to set up a timeline in 
which grievances in SAMADHAN portal no t redressed gets upgraded to 
CHAMPIONS portal with inbuilt mechanisms for penalising the persons 
responsible if the same is not redressed the CHAMPIONS portal within timeline 
defined.  
 

 
 
43 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee would like to be apprised of the grievances redressed 
through SAMADHAN Portal and CHAMPIONS Portal respectively and the 
reasons for non redressal of grievances even after the registration is done on 
CHAMPIONS Portal. The Committee further impress upon the M inistry to 
set u p a timeline within  which grievances in SAMADHAN Portal not 
redressed gets upgraded to CHAMPIONS Portal with inbuilt mechanisms for 
penalising the persons responsible if the same is not redressed in 
CHAMPIONS Portal within a timeline defined.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
41. The Committee notes that TReDS is a new initiative by the Ministry of 
MSME for resolving the problem of delayed payments to MSMEs by 
CPSEs/Government Agencies. Making penal provision of 1% per month for erring 
buyers will definitely prove to be a deterrent for defaulting buyers. The Committee 
expects that the penal provision is enforced in letter and spirit. The Committee 
hopes that TReDS will able to solve the problem of delayed payments and improve 
the liquidity position of  the MSMEs. The Committee recommends that TReDS 
should be implemented strictly and monitored regularly and the MSMEs may be 
exempted from paying charges for on -boarding this platform beyond 31 st March 
2021. 
(Para 79) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Presently, there is no such provision initiated by M/o MSME with respect to 
TReDS. However, this Ministry proposes to issue a notification related to TReDS 
which may include the enforcement and penal provisions relating to on  boarding 
and transacting on the TReDS platform. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee strongly feels that making penal provision of 1% per 
month for erring CPSEs will definitely prove to be a deterrent for default ing 
CPSEs.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that strict provisions against 
delayed payments need to be put in place to ensure timely release of 
payments by CPSEs which can immensely help the MSMEs to meet their 
working capital/credit  requirements for sustaining their businesses .  The 
Committee further recommends that necessary steps should also be taken for 

 
 
44 
 
issuance of notification in re spect of TReDS making penal provisions of 1% 
per month for defaulting CPSEs at the earliest.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
42. The Committee notes that the pace of expen diture under the NSCST Hub 
Scheme is not at all encouraging and that the allocation of Rs. 150 crores in the 
BE 2020-2021 has been reduced to Rs. 120 crores at the RE Stage. Further, the 
allocation for FY 2021-2022 has also been kept at Rs. 120 crores at t he BE Stage. 
The Committee fails to understand the reasons for such slow pace of expending in 
respect of such an important Scheme, which has been specially formulated for the 
marginalized section of the society. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should take adequate steps to speed up the spending process, so that allocated 
amount gets utilized to the optimum.  
(Para 84) 
 
Action Taken 
 
To develop entrepreneurship among SC/ST population and for maximum 
on-ground penetration, several interventions have been introduced since inception 
of National SC/ST Hub. With the increase of awareness of these interventions 
among targeted beneficiaries, the utilization of funds is increasing year to year. An 
allocation of Rs. 150 crores was earmarked in BE 2020 -21 under the Hub. 
However, due to the Covid -19 pandemic, the off take under the interventions of 
Hub was not at the expected level. Further, facilitation of SC/ST MSEs for their 
participation in International as well as domestic exhibitions could not be made  
during the year. However, the entire allocation of Rs. 120 crores made in RE 
2020-21 under the Scheme has been utilized. 
 
In BE 2021 -22, an amount of Rs. 150 crores has been allocated under the 
National SC/ST Hub. Several modifications to make the Scheme more inclusive 
and effective have been proposed under the SFC Notes for its continuation in next 
financial cycle. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 The Committee observes that despite claims being made by the 
Ministry of the success of National SC -ST Hub Scheme, negligible results are 
being seen at the ground level. The National SC -ST Hub Scheme was 
launched with the aim of promoting entrepreneurship culture among 
marginalized sections of the society but the desired results are not being seen.  

 
 
45 
 
The proc urement from SC/ST entrepreneurs has remained around            
0.69 per cent for FY 2021 -22 as against 4 per cent annual sub -target set for 
central ministries, departments and PSUs to procure from SC/ST MSEs, as 
reported on SAMBANDH portal of the M/o MSME and there has been a 
continuous decline over the previous years. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that concrete steps should be taken by the Ministry to ensure 
adequate participation of SC /ST entrepreneurs in the Public Procurement 
Policy and meeting 4 per cent target for procurement  from SC/ST MSEs .  
Further, Ministry should also ensure to spend the budgetary allocations 
earmarked for National SC-ST Hub Scheme in time-bound manner to ensure 
optimum budget utilization. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
46 
 
CHAPTER-IV 
 
Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
43. The Committee was apprised by the Ministry that besides 219 Districts, 56 
Aspirational Districts have also been covered under SFURTI. The Committee 
recommends that more attention should be paid to target more and more 
Aspirational Districts across the country as this can immensely improve the socio -
economic conditions of the inhabitants in those districts and improve the human 
development index. The Ministry may coordinate with the state governments and 
with concerted efforts desired results may be achieved .  
(Para 55) 
 
Action Taken 
 
As on 30.4.2021, 65 clusters have been approved in Aspirational Districts.  
Nodal Agencies under SFURTI Scheme have been advised to explore the 
possibility of setting up more clusters in the Aspirational Districts.

 2 
CHAPTER – I 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee was informed that the Delhi -Chandigarh E -vehicle friendly 
expressway has been completed and declared as the first e -vehicle friendly expressway of 
the Country. The work was under progress in another two expressways/highways viz., 
Delhi - Jaipur and Mumbai - Pune. DHI further informed that 22 charging stations have 
been installed on the Delhi - Jaipur Expressway and work is going on for installation of 
another 10 charging stations. Similarly, 11 charging stations have been installed on the 
Mumbai - Pune expressways and work is in progress for installing another 6 charging 
stations. The Department assured that the installation work on these charging stations 
would be completed within a few months after the lifting of lock -down. As the lock -down 
has now been lifted across the country, the Committee desires that the installation of the 
remaining Charging Stations on the Delhi - Jaipur and Mumbai -Pune 
Highways/expressways may be completed expeditiously and the Committee be apprised 
of the completion.  
(Para 29) 
 Action Taken Replies 
 As on 30th September, 2021, 29 charging stations have been installed on the Delhi 
- Jaipur-Agra Expressway/Highways and work is going on for installation of another 3 
charging stations. Similarly, 15 charging stations have  been installed on the Mumbai - 
Pune expressways and work is in progress for installing another 2 charging stations.  The 
work for installing charging stations on the sanctioned expressways/ highways is in 
progress. The installation work of sanctioned charg ing stations would be completed 
expeditiously as normalcy gets restored. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.            The future of the automobile Industry is going to be influenced by the next 
generation autonomous driving technology. The next generation aut onomous driving 
technology is currently in the development and testing phase in the developed nations. It 
would rather enhance road safety and reduce road accidents, pollutions and carbon 
emissions, fuel consumption, road congestion, make transportation ac cessible to all 
including disabled. The Committee has been informed that the autonomous vehicles are 
in different levels, with level 0 being the manual cars of today and level 5 the fully 

 3 
autonomous, self -driven vehicles. The Committee is aware of a few de merits of 
autonomous vehicles in Indian environment owing to the heavy traffic and poor road 
conditions, more so as it will affect the employment of Drivers. In India, some 
manufacturers are now introducing level 1 autonomous vehicle. OEMs are working on 
R&D and would be launching different levels of vehicles with autonomous functionality 
in the near future. The Indian automobile industry has a stake on the global Auto Sector 
and hence any lag may leave us behind in the race. To keep pace with the latest 
technology, the Committee expects that necessary initiative in this regard is taken to 
promote autonomous driving technology to compete with the international market trends. 
    
 (Para 38) 
Action Taken Replies 
Autonomous vehicles will be encouraged. 
In order  to ensure that Indian manufacturers keep pace with the Global auto 
manufacturers, the Automotive Industry Standards (AIS) Committee has already initiated 
the formulation work for the following aspects of autonomous driving technology viz., 
Auto Emergency Braking (AEB) for Commercial vehicles application, and Lane 
departure system. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee accordingly opines that the Ministry may scale up the technology 
and infrastructure of the Scheme. For the said purpose, it may do gr ound level 
assessment of the requirements when scaling-up needs. The Committee notes that the M/o 
Finance have provided BE of Rs.97.59 crore for the Scheme, which was the projected 
demand made by the Ministry. However, for scaling up, more funds would be r equired 
and the same may be placed before the M/o Finance at the RE 2020-21 stage. 
(Para 57) 
Action Taken Replies 
The scheme enhancement of competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector

replacement of old vehicles with newer ones. MoRTH has taken out the  following 
notifications:

Scrapping Facility) Rules, 2021 for establishment of Registered Vehicles Scrapping 
Facility (RVSF). 
 
ii) Draft GSR Notification 177(E) dt 12.03.2021-

Vehicles would be non-renewable on lapse of 15 years.

 The Dr aft Notification provides for revision of registration fee, fitness testing fee and 
fitness certification fee of vehicles. The initiative is towards creation of an ecosystem for

v) Draft GSR Notification 278(E)  dt 08.04.2021-  
The Draft Notification provides for recognition, regulation and control of Automated 
Testing Station. 
  
 
 

 32

 The Committee finds from the reply of the Ministry that there is no mention 
of Voluntary Vehicle Scrapping Policy. More over, the Notifications are  silent on
