Recommendation/Observation 
38. As part of examination of the DFG 2021 -22, some of the Automobile Association 
had submitted before the Committee the following concerns and  challenges facing the 
Industry that requires attention of the Government. The Committee recommends that DHI 
may suitably intervene with the Ministries concerned for addressing these issues:  
 Acute shortage of steel being supplied by domestic suppliers, le ading to increase 
in steel prices in the Country.  
 Acute shortage of containers and significant increase in price of international 
logistics.  
 Mandatory certification of some of the components like Safety Glass (for QCO) 
has been enforced. The implementati on of QCO for Safety Glass has deferred 
partially till 1st April, 2021 which needs to be extended further.  
 Implementation of Quality Control Orders (QCOs) and BIS licensing for auto 
components.  
 Hardships being faced due to delay in customs clearance post  implementation of 
CAROTAR.  
 Surge in price because of implementation of BS-VI emission norms.  
 Shortage of semiconductor and chips  
 To make Dealer's entire Auto Business (Dealership + Workshop) a part of 
MSME. Presently only 2 wheeler and passenger vehicl e dealers workshops are 
under MSME. 3 wheeler, commercial vehicle, tractors and construction 
equipment categories also needs to be included in MSME category.

of defining their land use as both commercial and factory land.

 35 
Further, it is informed that Automobile Wheel Rim Component (Quality Control) 
Order, 2020 was issued by the Ministry of Heavy Industries .   The implementation date

Recommendation/Observation 
39. The Committee has been informed by the Auto Associations that the fast -tracking 
of emissions and fuel efficiency in India has resulted in large investments  and cost 
increase. Further the two big regulations which include CAFE Phase 2 and BS VI phase 
2 are to be implemented from April, 2022 and April, 2023 respectively. These regulations 
will have major economic impact leading to further cost increase affecti ng adversely the 
already stressed automobile industry. The per capita income of our country has not 
increased in the same tandem as the increase in cost. It was further informed that the 
Indian fuel emission standards are now equivalent to standards of man y automobile 
manufacturing countries globally and the fuel emission levels have gone down and also 
the fuel efficiency has improved significantly. The Auto Associations, therefore, suggested 
for deferment of the following emission regulations. The Committe e, with a view to boost 
the struggling Automotive Sector, the following suggestions of the Automobile 
Associations for temporary deferment in the emission regulations is forwarded for 
consideration of the Government:  
 
 BS VI Phase 2 Emission regulations, i ncluding RDE and PEMS which are 
notified for implementation from 1st April, 2023 may be deferred to 1st April, 
2024 for new models and 1st April, 2025 for existing models.  
 Phase 2 Fuel Efficiency Regulations for Passenger Vehicles notified for 
implementation from 1st April, 2022 may be deferred for implementation from 1st 
April, 2024.  
 Fuel Efficiency Regulation for Light, Medium and Heavy - Duty BS VI vehicles 
may also be implemented from 1st April, 2024.  
 OBD II Regulation for two Wheelers and three Whee lers scheduled for 1st April, 
2023 may be deferred and implemented in two phases, 1st Phase from 1st April, 2024 
and 2nd Phase from 1st April, 2026. 
 
(Para 37) 
 
 
 

 36 
Action Taken Replies 
It is informed that suggestions received directly from Automobiles Assoc iations 
regarding deferment in the emission regulations have been forwarded to the concerned 
Ministry/Department for favourable consideration.    Present recommendations of the 
Committee have also been shared with them. 
 
Background: 
 
(a)  India has submitte d its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) in 2015 for 
the implementation of Paris Agreement in the post 2020 period. The NDC has 8 goals, 
including 3 quantitative goals, one of which is: reduction in emission intensity of Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP) by 33% to 35% by 2030 from 2005 levels. 
(b) Government has set a target of reducing import of crude oil by 10% for the year 
2022. 
(c) Ministry is trying to align Indian automotive standards to European standards for 
enhancing India‟s global competitiveness. 
(d) There is a dire need to reduce air pollution. 
CAFÉ Norms (Fuel Efficiency for Passenger vehicles) 
 
In order to meet the global commitment, the Ministry of Power, under the Energy 
Conservation Act, issued notification S.O. 1072(e) 23 rd April 2015 to e nsure that motor 
vehicle types approved under Central Motor Vehicle Rules (CMVR) 1989 up to 3.5 tons 
gross vehicle weight follow the energy consumption standard for the purpose of 
manufacturing or importing for sale in the following manner:- 
 
 Each manufac turer shall comply with Energy consumption standard in the 
following phases: (i) The 1st phase was applicable from 1st April 2017 to 31st March 2022 
with a target CO 2 Emission of 13 gm/km. (ii) The second phase, effective from 1 st April 
2022, laid a target of CO2 emission equal to 113 gm/km. 
 
Therefore 7 years of preparation lead time was given to the auto manufacturers in mutual 
agreement with all the stake holders, including the automobile industry. 
 
Global Experience: 
The target of Japan for the year 2020 was 115gm/km. 
The European Union has set a target of 95gm/km for 2021. 
 

 37 
Fuel Efficiency norms for Light, Medium and Heavy Duty Motor Vehicles 
Fuel Efficiency norms have not been implemented so far. 
 
Inter-Ministerial Committee under MoPNG has already fin alized the fuel 
efficiency norms. However, due to BS VI and revision of axle loads, the correction 
factors have been finalized with the participation of the industry. It is under approval. 
 
Real Driving Emissions (RDE): 
To reduce emission performance gap o f vehicles between lab and real driving 
conditions, Real Driving Emission (RDE) regulation was introduced with Bharat Stage 
VI (BS VI) norms, vide GSR 889(E) dated 16 th Sept. 2016. India also made RDE 
measurement mandatory during type approval and COP (Con formity of production) 
applicable from 1 st April, 2020 for data collection and from 1 st April, 2023 for meeting 
Conformity factor (CF). Europe has made these regulations applicable from September, 
2017. Therefore, sufficient lead time has been given to the  automotive industry to meet 
the timeline. 
 
On Board Diagnostics 
 
On-board diagnostics („OBD‟) is essential for timely repair and maintenance of 
vehicle. It is required to review the list of devices monitored for electric circuit 
malfunctions, including excess emissions. 
 
OBD requirements for BS-VI compliant 2W in India 
OBD system specifications for two-wheelers have been included for the first time 
in the BS VI regulation in September 2016. 
 
India has introduced OBD -I for Wheelers from 1 st April 2020. The applicable 
requirements are circuit continuity checks, MIL (Malfunction Indicator Lamp) 
requirement, electrical disconnection of EVAP (Evaporative purge control) system and 
EGR (Exhaust Gas Recirculation) monitoring. 
 
OBD-II goes a step ahead. Apart from O BD-I requirement, it proposes to include 
catalytic converter monitoring, misfire detection and oxygen sensor monitoring for 
deterioration along with OBD threshold emission requirements. The requirements of 2W 
OBD I and II are summarized in the table below:-

OBD II Threshold limits: 
The OBD system shall indicate the failure of an emission -related component or 
system when that failure results in emissions exceeding the OBD emission threshold 
limits of CO (Carbon Monoxide), NMHC (Non -methane hydrocarbons) and NOx 
(Nitrogen Oxide). 
 
Conclusion: 
Due to global commitments, to reduce air pollution, to align with global standards 
and with sufficient time having already been given to the automobile industry, it would 
be challenging to extend the deadline. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
40. The GST rates on automobiles are at the highest level of 28%. Indian industry 
and suppliers have invested significant resources to migrate to BS -VI. As far as two -
wheelers are concerned, in leapfrogging from BS -IV to BS -VI, Industry has recorded a 
35% increase in cost in the last quarters. Small engine size two -wheelers are used by a 
major population of self -employed, entrepreneurial common people. Hence there is need 
to consider the affordability for end -customer. Reduction in GST rate would help 
sustained growth in the industry and accelerate the adoption of BS -VI and improve GST 
collection accruing from increased sale. The Committee, therefore, recommends that to 
improve affordability of the customers and simultaneously boost the automobile sector, 
the GST rate on all segments may be reduced from 28% to 18%. The decreased GST rate 
would prove to be an impetus to enhance the sales and thereby, would offset the losses, if 
any, to the Exchequer kitty.  
(Para 39) 

 39 
Action Taken Replies 
To overcome the issu es faced by the automotive industry, Department had a 
meeting with leaders of the auto industry SIAM, ACMA and several OEMs 
manufacturers for suggestions. Department has forwarded the recommendation to the 
Department of Revenue for reduction of GST.

41. The Committee notes that presently, there is no parity in the Road Tax imposed by 
different States. The Committee has been informed that the MoRTH has been discussing 
this issue with States and is proposing an agenda of “One Natio n One Tax” as per the

benefit of the people across the country.

Revival and Mill Development Plan (RMDP)  of NEPA Ltd. which was slated to be

of the implementation of the RMDP. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts 
should be made on a priority basis to complete the RMDP of NEPA expeditiously. A 
compliance report on this aspect may be furnished to the Committee.  
(Para 90) 
 

 40

Recommendation/Observation 
 
1. Also the Committee was informed about the key observations of the study 
which was that the small businesses were worst hit by the economic fallout of Co vid-
19 Pandemic. Unprecedented lockdown and other containment measures have 
resulted in supply chain disruptions and massive demand drop especially for Micro 
units and significant economic losses in general to MSMEs. Further as per the 
survey data, 88 per cent of the beneficiaries of PMEGP units reported that they were 
negatively affected due to Covid -19 Pandemic and the remaining 12 per cent stated 
that they were not affected. In terms of beneficiaries (88 per cent) who were 
negatively affected, around 57 per cent stated that their units were shut down during 
this period, 30 per cent reported that there was drop in production and revenue, 28 
per cent stated issues pertaining to raw material availability or supply chain issues. 
In terms of beneficiaries (12 per cent) who were positively affected, around 65 per 
cent stated that there is an increase in business activity as they had units in retail 
and health sector, 53 per cent stated an increase in telephonic supply/delivery and 
around 25 per cent stated that their units were dealing with essential commodities or 
services. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take immediate 
suitable action to rescue the small business units from collapsing, by providing 
additional financial support, relaxation or w aiver of interest, marketing support,  
etc.  
(Para 50) 
Action taken 
 
The Reserve Bank has announced the following relief measures for MSMEs 
adversely affected by the outbreak of the pandemic:  
(i) Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector – Restructuring of 
Advances: With a view to facilitate meaningful restructuring of stressed MSME 
accounts a one -time restructuring of loans to MSMEs that were in default but 
‘standard’ as on January 1, 2019 , was permitted, without an asset classification 
downgrade, vide our circular dated January 1, 2019, subject to certain conditions. 
The scheme was extended vide circular dated February 11, 2020 to stressed MSMEs 
loans that were ‘standard’ as on January 1, 2020 subject to certain conditions 

 
 
3 
 
including implementation of restructuring by December 31, 2020. In view of the 
need to support the viable MSME entities on account of the fallout of COVID -19, 
the scheme has been extended for restructuring of advances whe re the borrower’s 
account was a ‘standard asset’ as on March 1, 2020 and aggregate exposure was up 
to Rs. 25 crore. The restructuring under this scheme had to be implemented by 
March 31, 2021. This scheme permits banks to upgrade such accounts as ‘standard  
asset’ upon implementation of the restructuring plan which may have slipped into 
NPA category between March 2, 2020 and date of implementation.  
 
(ii) Resolution Framework for COVID -19-related Stress: Stressed MSME units 
having exposure of more than Rs. 25 cror e may avail benefits under RBI circular 
dated August 6, 2020 on Resolution Framework for COVID -19-related Stress which 
has permitted a window under the Prudential Framework to enable the lenders to 
implement a resolution plan in respect of eligible corpora te exposures without 
change in ownership while classifying such exposures as standard subject to 
specified conditions. Under the guidelines, provisions have been made for inter alia 
allowing extension of the residual tenor of the loan, with or without paym ent 
moratorium, by a period not more than two years as well as providing additional 
funding based on viability considerations. 
 
Further, in view of the resurgence of Covid -19, the Reserve Bank has 
announced the Resolution Framework 2.0 dated May 05, 2021 s ubsequently revised 
on June 04, 2021 which permits lending institutions to restructure the advances to 
MSME borrowers, which could not be restructured under earlier schemes, without a 
downgrade in the asset classification subject to the conditions specifie d in the 
Resolution Framework 2.0. The facility is available to MSME borrowers having 
aggregate exposure, including non -fund based facilities, of all lending institutions 
not exceeding 50 core INR as on March 31, 2021 and shall have to be invoked by 
September 30, 2021. 
 
Even in respect of MSME accounts restructured under earlier schemes, 
lending institutions have been permitted, as a one -time measure, to review the 
working capital sanctioned limits and / or drawing power based on a reassessment of 
the working capital cycle, reduction of margins, etc. without the same being treated 
as restructuring. 
 

 
 
4 
 
(iii) Rescheduling of Payments and other reliefs on account of Covid -19 Pandemic 
under Covid-19 Regulatory Package– Term Loans and Working Capital Facilities 
 
a) All comm ercial banks (including regional rural banks, small finance banks 
and local area banks), co -operative banks, all -India Financial Institutions, and 
NBFCs (including housing finance companies and micro -finance institutions) were 
permitted to allow a moratorium of six months on payment of installments in respect 
of all term loans outstanding as on March 1, 2020. 
 
b) In respect of working capital facilities sanctioned in the form of cash 
credit/overdraft, lending institutions were permitted to allow a deferment of  six 
months on payment of interest in respect of all such facilities outstanding as on 
March 1, 2020. The accumulated interest for the period would be paid after the 
expiry of the deferment period. Alternatively, the lenders could convert the 
accumulated interest into a funded interest term loan payable by not later than March 
31, 2021. 
 
c) In respect of working capital facilities sanctioned in the form of cash 
credit/overdraft, lending institutions were allowed to recalculate drawing power by 
reducing margins and/or by reassessing the working capital cycle for the borrowers.  
 
(iv) Loans against Gold Ornaments and Jewellery for Non -Agricultural End-uses: 
Loan-to-value ratio (LTV) was temporarily increased from 75 per cent to 90 per cent 
till March 31, 2021 for loans  against gold ornaments and jewellery for non -
agricultural end -uses. Fresh gold loans sanctioned on and after April 1, 2021 shall 
attract LTV ratio of 75 per cent as hitherto. 
 
(v) Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS): Government of India 
has launched Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) for business 
including MSMEs and the scheme is being implemented by National Credit 
Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC). As credit facilities extended under the 
scheme guaranteed by NCGTC are backed by an unconditional and irrevocable 
guarantee provided by GoI, Member Lending Institutions (SCBs including 
scheduled RRBs), NBFCs (including HFCs as eligible under the scheme) and AIFIs) 
have been permitted to apply zero percent risk weight on the credit faci lities 
extended under this scheme to the extent of guarantee coverage. A circular in this 
regard has been issued by RBI on June 21, 2020. 
 

 
 
5 
 
(vi)  Credit Guarantee Scheme for Subordinate Debt (CGSSD): GoI has launched 
Distressed Assets Fund Scheme for providing s ubordinate debt to stressed MSMEs. 
The scheme is being implemented by Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and 
Small Enterprises (CGTMSE). As the credit facilities extended under the scheme are 
backed by a guarantee from CGTMSE, as a special dispensation,  banks were 
permitted to reckon the funds infused by the promoters in their MSME units through 
loans availed under the above scheme as equity/quasi equity from the promoters for 
debt-equity computation. A circular in this regard has been issued on July 1, 2020. 
 
(vii) In order to reduce the cost of credit to MSME and to encourage incremental 
lending to the sector, the threshold for exposures which qualify as regulatory retail 
portfolio and attracts a lower risk weight of 75%, was increased from Rs.5 crore to 
Rs.7.5 crore on October 12, 2020. Generally, unrated exposures attract a risk weight 
of 100%. 
 
(viii) In order to incentivi ze new credit flow to the micro, small, and medium 
enterprise (MSME) borrowers, Scheduled Commercial Banks have been allowed to 
deduct credit di sbursed to ‘New MSME borrowers’ from their Net Demand and 
Time Liabilities (NDTL) for calculation of the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). This 
exemption is available only up to ₹25 lakh per borrower disbursed up to the fortnight 
ending December 31, 2021 for a per iod of one year from the date of origination of 
the loan or the tenure of the loan, whichever is earlier.

materials on time and at reasonable price. Traders are hoarding the raw materials 
and rigging the market with their whims and fancy pricin g. The Committee 
recommends that NSIC should make suitable arrangements so that raw materials 
are made easily available at reasonable price for Micro enterprises, on credit basis.

Government for the economic revival from  the Pandemic hit economy has been 
found to be inadequate as the measures adopted were more of loan offering and

Enterprises due to Covid -19 Pandemic. Unlike Large and Medium enterprises, 
Small enterprises depend on regular cash flows to stay afloat. The Committee,

 In order to help the Micro and Small Enterprises get  higher access to 
institutional Credit, following are the measures undertaken by Government:

a) Ministry of MSME and Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) had 
jointly set up Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micr o and Small Enterprises 
(CGTMSE) in the year 2000. CGTMSE provides guarantee to Member Lending 
Institutions (MLIs) for credit facilities sanctioned by them to Micro and Small 
Entrepreneurs (MSEs) without collateral security and third party guarantee up to Rs. 
2 crore. During the year 2020 -21, the trust has extended guarantees to 8.35 lakh loan 
accounts, amounting to Rs 36,899 crore. The Trust has taken multiple initiatives 
during the last few years to make the scheme more accessible to the MSEs.    
b) The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) has been formulated as a 
relief measure to MSMEs by providing them additional funding of up to Rs. 3 lakh 
crore in the form of a fully guaranteed emergency credit line. Borrowers with up to 
Rs. 25 crore outstanding  and Rs. 100 crore turnover are eligible. This scheme 
provides 100 per cent credit guarantee cover to Banks and NBFCs on principal and 
interest. No guarantee fee and fresh collateral is required.  
c)  Provision made for Rs. 20,000 crore subordinate debt for M SMEs which are NPAs 
or are stressed. Government to support them with Rs. 4,000 crore to Credit 
Guarantee Trust for Micro and Small enterprises (CGTMSE). Banks are expected to 
provide the subordinate -debt to promoters of such MSMEs equal to 15 per cent of 
the existing stake in the unit subject to a maximum of Rs. 75 lakhs.  
d)  Government has set up a Fund of Funds with a corpus of Rs. 10,000 crore that will 
provide equity funding support of Rs.  50,000 crore for MSMEs. The Fund of Funds 
shall be operated throug h a mother and multiple daughter funds. It will provide 
equity funding for viable MSMEs. This scheme will help MSMEs to expand its size 
and capacity and will also encourage them to get listed on stock exchanges.  
e)  Income tax refunds to nearly 8.2 lakh smal l businesses worth Rs. 5,204 crore 
have been issued with the objective to help MSMEs to carry on their business 
activities without pay cuts and layoffs in these challenging times.  
f) Government will   provide Interest subvention of 2 per cent to prompt payees  for a 
period of 12 months which will benefit Small business under MUDRA. The total 
relief is expected to be to the tune of Rs. 1500 crore.

10. The Committee is of the view that the 90 days limit fixed by RBI for classifying 
overdues of MSMEs should be increased to 180 days so that MSMEs are not 
constrained to divert their working capital towards servicing of their loan -
instalments and clearing th eir dues at the cost of normal business operations. This 
proposed change in the RBI guidelines will save a large number of MSMEs from 
turning sick or getting closed resulting in loss of economic activity and employment. 
It will also prevent avoidable class ification of bad debts and unwarranted litigation 
by banks, thereby saving the banks too, from losses.  
(Para 41) 
 
Action taken 
 
The extant asset classification norms of RBI which stipulate 90 -days past due 
(DPD) requirement for declaring an account as NPA  were issued based on the 
recommendations of the Financial Sector Reforms Committee (Chair: Shri  
Narasimham) after extensive deliberations and based on best international practices. 
Most of the jurisdictions around the world, particularly all the G20 count ries, follow 
the same norm of 90 days for classification as NPA, which has also been enshrined 
as part of Basel guidelines. 
 
The current norms constitute one of the key pillars of the prudential regulation 
and diluting the same will have broader financial stability implications. 
Classification of a borrower account as NPA by lending institutions is merely a 
formal, albeit delayed, recognition of the underlying stress in the borrower accounts 
and any dilution of the same will only delay the process of resolu tion of the stress in 
borrower accounts. Doing so will ultimately impair the financial health of the 
banking system and constrain their lending ability. 
 
Moreover, merely changing the criteria for recognition of an asset as non -
performing may not solve the financial stress associated with the exposure. 

 
 
19 
 
Resolution of financial stress involves recognition of stress as the first step, which 
may entail the lending institution having to recognize the losses incurred. 
 
Recommendation/Observation

13. MSMEs are finding it difficult to procure raw material to run their businesses 
normally due to non -availability of raw materials. Moreover, a steep hike in the 
prices of raw material like steel etc. has adversely affected the business 
environment. The Committee recommends that the Public Sector Enterprises should 
not impose penalty or black list the MSMEs in the event of cancellation of orders by 
them since increase in prices of raw materials is a Force Majeure event, beyond the 
control of the MSMEs. Besides, the Government should also allow import of all steel 
materials based on cost and quality requirements at zero import duty (no anti -
dumping) and also ban export of iron ore and steel products for the time being. 
Better GDP growth can be realized only if value-added products are exported rather 
than raw materials. Further, GST -based funding is needed for MSMEs at marginal 
rates, which will encourage them to purchase raw materials easily.  
 
(Para 58)

Action taken 
 
Steel is a deregulated sector where prices are a function of demand and 
supply, global market conditions, trends in price of raw materials, logistics cost, 
power and fuel cost etc. The factors contributing to increase in price of steel over the 
last one ye ar include demand -supply mismatch following Covid -19 led lockdown, 
disruption in supply chains, logistics, availability of human resources, raw materials 
and working capital etc., reduced availability of steel across the globe during the 
pandemic leading t o global increase in iron ore and steel prices and reduced 
availability of iron ore domestically due to non -operationalization of working mines 
in Odisha post auction in March 2020. 
 
The Government has also taken steps to ramp up production of iron ore and  
steel to increase their domestic availability so as to offset the impact due to price 
which include increasing availability of iron ore through Mining and Mineral Policy 
reforms to enhance production and availability of iron ore, ramping up production 
and maximum capacity utilization by government mining companies, grant of 
permission to Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) to sell 25% fresh fines and 70 
Million Ton dumps and tailings, accelerating auction of iron -ore fines by SAIL and 
early operational ization of forfeited working mines of Odisha by the State and 
Central Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) etc. 
 
In Union Budget 2021-22, Customs Duty has been reduced uniformly to 7.5% 
on Semis, Flat and Long products of non -alloy, alloy and stainless steels . Further, to 
provide relief to metal re -cyclers, mostly MSMEs, BCD on steel scrap has been 
exempted for a period up to 31 stMarch 2022. In addition to the above, anti-dumping 
duty (ADD) and countervailing duty (CVD) on certain steel products have also been 
revoked / temporarily revoked. 
 
Keeping in view the overall interest of the domestic steel sector, blanket ban 
on imposition of Anti -dumping duty and complete ban on export of iron ore and 
steel may not be a feasible proposition in a de -regulated and diversified steel sector. 
Considering all aspects, Government makes required adjustments in Export/Import 
duty and takes safeguard measures from time to time.  
 
The Nationa l Steel Policy  (NSP), 2017 aims at inter -alia achieving a wider 
presence globally in value added/ high grade steel. The Government has approved a 
Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Specialty Steel to boost the domestic 

 
 
23 
 
production of ‘Specialty St eel’ and attract significant investment for production of 
‘Specialty Steel’ in the country. It will help the Indian steel industry mature in terms 
of technology as well as move up the value chain.

Besides, Government has taken a slew of relief measures for the benefit of

losses suffered by the MSME Sector as a whole due to nationwide lockdown imposed 
by the Govern ment. More so, the second wave of the Pandemic exposed the 
vulnerabilities of MSMEs like never before and highlighted the problems faced by 
them such as delayed payments, high informality, low financial resilience, scarcity 
in raw material availability etc . The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that a 
detailed study needs to be conducted to make an assessment of the actual losses 
suffered by the MSME Sector so as to chalk out an effective plan for revival of the 
MSME Sector, which has the potential to  contribute significantly in achieving the 
much coveted target of making India a $5 trillion economy.   
(Para 25) 
 
Action taken 
 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) had assigned the task of 
conducting a National level evaluation of the PMEGP Scheme to Deloitte Touche 
Tohmatsu India LLP.  The agency had submitted the report in September, 2020.  
 
Key Observations:  
 
 Small businesses were hit by the economic fallout of COVID -19 pandemic. 
Lockdown and other containment measures resulted in supply chain 
disruptions and demand drop  especially for micro units.  The containment 
measures taken to check the spread of pandemic led to significant economic 
losses to MSME units. 
Units affected by COVID-19 pandemic: 
 

 
 
32

26. The Committee observes that the directions issued by the Government of India

recommends that  provisions contained in Chapter V of MSMED Act, 2006

strengthen MSME Sector in the country.

30. It has also been observed that MSMEs do not publish their invoices on TReDS 
platform despite having the registration  due to unsaid pressure from corporate 
(buyers). Further , it is seen that corporate (buyers) do not approve the published 
invoices of MSMEs on TReDS platform, which defies the sole purpose of the 
platform, as Banks cannot fund such invoices. The Committee is of the view that 
every tax invoice raised by GST registered MSMEs should reflect automatically on 
the respective TReDS platforms. After the delivery of Services or Goods, within a 
certain number of days, the corporate must accept or reject the automatic ally 
published invoice of MSMEs. After the stipulated period, the published invoice 
should be deemed accepted and should be available for banks to provide fund to 
MSMEs. If the CPSEs rejects any invoice, a mandatory clarification must be sought 
which shoul d be visible to Banks and respective MSMEs. Consequently, MSMEs 
would be encouraged to get themselves registered on GST and TReDS Platforms as 
their invoices would automatically get published on TReDS which would open the 
doors for them to have access to e asy and cheaper funds. It would also provide 
significant business potential for banks due to rise in number of invoices available 
on TReDS. The Committee feels that it would also make CPSEs responsible and 
cautious while rejecting any invoice raised by MSM Es and help them financially in 
this critical juncture. The proposal if implemented, would thereby, become a win -
win situation to MSMEs, CPSEs and Banks as each one of them are likely to benefit.   
 
(Para 62)

Enterprises (DPE) has also advised all the administrative Ministries/ Departments on

ANNEXURE- I 
Measures taken so far to support MSMEs 
 
A. Atmanirbhar Bharat  
1. ₹ 3 lakh crores Collateral -free Automatic Loans for Businesses, including 
MSMEs: The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) has been 
formulated as a relief measure to MSMEs by providing them additional funding 
of up to ₹ 3 lakh crore in the form of a fully guaranteed emergency credit line. 
Borrowers with up to ₹ 25 crore outstanding and ₹ 100 crore turnover are 
eligible. This scheme provides 100 per cent credit guarantee cover to Banks and 
NBFCs on principal and interest. No guarantee fee, no fresh collateral is required.  
2. ₹20,000 crore Subordinate D ebt for Stressed MSMEs : Provision made for ₹ 
20,000 crore subordinate debt for MSMEs which are NPAs or are stressed. 
Government to support them with ₹ 4,000 crore to Credit Guarantee Trust for 
Micro and Small enterprises (CGTMSE). Banks are expected to pro vide the 
subordinate-debt to promoters of such MSMEs equal to 15 per cent of the 
existing stake in the unit subject to a maximum of ₹ 75 lakhs.  
3. ₹ 50,000 crores equity infusion through MSME Fund of Funds:  Government to 
set up a Fund of Funds with a corpus of ₹ 10,000 crore that will provide equity 
funding support for MSMEs. The Fund of Funds shall be operated through a 
mother and a few daughter funds. It will provide equity funding for viable 
MSMEs. This scheme will help MSMEs to expand its size and capacit y and will 
also encourages them to get listed on stock exchanges.  
4. New definition of MSME: Low threshold in MSME definition have created a fear 
among MSMEs of graduating out of the benefits. Hence, government has revised 
definition of MSME by raising the I nvestment limit. An additional criteria of 
turnover has been introduced and distinction between manufacturing and service 
sector stands removed.  
5. Global tenders to be disallowed upto ₹ 200 crores:  General Financial Rules 
(GFR) of the Government amended to disallow global tender enquiries in 
government procurement of goods and services of value of less than ₹ 200 crores. 
This is a step in support of the Make in India initiative and will promote MSMEs 
to grow.  
6. Other Measures for MSMEs: e-market linkage for M SMEs to act as a 
replacement for trade fairs and exhibitions. MSME receivables from Government 

 
 
48 
 
and CPSEs to be released in 45 days. This would help MSMEs to solve the 
problems of marketing and liquidity.  
7. Income Tax Refund:  Income tax refunds to nearly 8.2  lakh small businesses 
worth ₹ 5,204 crore has been issued with the objective to help MSMEs to carry 
on their business activities without pay cuts and layoffs in these challenging 
times. 
8. Relief of ₹ 1500 crores to MUDRA - Shishu loans: GoI to provide Intere st 
subvention of 2 per cent to prompt payees for a period of 12 months. Small 
business under MUDRA to be benefited. 
9. Ease of doing business for business including MSMEs : Government announced 
further enhancement of Ease of Doing business through Insolvency a nd 
Bankruptcy Code (IBC) related measures which include (a). raising of the 
minimum threshold to initiate insolvency proceedings to Rs. 1 crore from Rs. 1 
lakh (which largely insulates MSMEs), (b) special insolvency resolution 
framework for MSMEs under Sec tion 240A of the Code, (c) suspension of fresh 
initiation of insolvency proceedings up to one year depending upon the pandemic 
situation and (d) empowering Central Government to exclude COVID 19 related 
debt from the definition of “default” under the Code for the purpose of triggering 
insolvency proceedings.  
10. Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro Finance Institutions:  Guarantee to be 
provided to Scheduled Commercial Banks for loans to new or existing NBFC -
MFIs or MFIs for on lending upto  Rs 1.25 lakh to approximately 25 lakh small 
borrowers. Loans from banks to be capped at Marginal Cost of Funds based 
Lending Rate (MCLR) plus 2%. Maximum loan tenure will be 3 years, and 80% 
of assistance to be used by MFI for incremental lending. Interest rates will be a t 
least 2% below maximum rate prescribed by RBI. Guarantee cover will be 
available for funding provided by MLIs to MFIs/NBFC -MFIs till March 31, 2022 
or till guarantees for an amount of Rs. 7,500 crore are issued, whichever is 
earlier. 
11. Udyam Registration P ortal-The Udyam registration Portal has facility through 
which an entrepreneur can opt for linking itself with Government e -market 
(GeM) place. With this facility, MSEs can link themselves with the 
Government’s procurement system and can participate in Gov ernment’s 
mandatory procurement program from MSEs. In addition to it, the portal has 
linkages with IT, GST and TReDs portals. In this regard, the Public Procurement 
Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE) Order 2012  had mandated every 

 
 
49 
 
Central Ministry /Department/PSU to set an annual goal for procurement of 
minimum 25% from the MSE sector. In addition, the Public Preference (Make in 
India) Order 2017 has mandated manufacturing, production of goods and services 
in India, in which preference for local man ufacturers and service providers and 
local content requirement is supporting public procurement from local suppliers, 
especially by MSMEs. 
12. Government of India on 02.07.2021 decided to include Retail and Wholesale 
Trade as MSMEs and they are allowed to be registered on UDYAM registration 
portal. However, benefits to the MSMEs engaged in Retail and Wholesale Trade 
would be restricted to availin g credit under Priority Sector Lending only. This 
measure will benefit a large number of trading entities.  
13. The World Bank has approved a loan of $500 million to support Government of 
India’s programme “Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP)” 
aimed at revitalizing the MSME sector, which has been heavily impacted by the 
COVID -19 pandemic. The Cabinet approval for the same is under process. 
RAMP is a part of the COVID Resilience and Recovery initiatives of the 
Government. The program aims at improv ing market access, access to credit, 
strengthening Institutions and governance at the Central and State level. The 
programme will support the ongoing support programmes of the Government, 
focusing on competitive aspect of MSMEs. It would enhance MSME 
performance through capacity building, handholding, skill development, quality 
enrichment, technological upgradation, digitization, outreach and marketing 
promotion through delivery of higher quality integrated services.  
14. Amendments to the Factoring Regulation A ct 2011 have been approved by 
Parliament which will enhance supply of credit to MSMEs from NBFCs.  
15. Government, on 23.10.2020, approved the Scheme for grant of ex -gratia payment 
of difference between compound interest and simple interest for six months, to 
borrowers in specified loan accounts. 
 
B. Union Budget for 2021-22 
1. To ensure faster resolution of cases, NCLT framework to be strengthened,             
e-Courts system shall be implemented and alternate methods of debt resolution 
and special framework for MSMEs shall be introduced.    
2. Budgetary allocation for MSMEs  of Rs. 15,700 crores provided in 2021 -22, 
which is more than double of BE for 2020-21.    

 
 
50 
 
3. Customs duty have been reduced uniformly  to 7.5% on semis, flat, and long 
products of non -alloy, alloy, and s tainless steels to provide relief to metal re -
cyclers, mostly MSMEs, Duty on steel scrap has been exempted for a period up 
to 31st March, 2022.  
4. Basic Customs Duty rates have been uniformly reduced  on caprolactam, nylon 
chips and nylon fiber & yarn to 5%. This will help the textile industry, MSMEs, 
and exports, too. 
5. Certain customs duty changes to benefit MSMEs have been made. Duty 
increased from 10% to 15% on steel screws and plastic builder wares. On prawn 
feed it is increased from  5%  to  15%.  Exemptio n  on  import  of  duty -free  
items  is rationalised as  an incentive  to  exporters  of 36 garments,  leather,  and  
handicraft  items.  Almost all these  items are made  domestically by MSMEs.  
Exemption  are withdrawn on imports  of certain  kind  of  lea thers  as  they  are  
domestically  produced  in  good  quantity and  quality,  mostly  by  MSMEs.  
Customs  duty  on  finished synthetic  gem  stones  is increased to  encourage  
their  domestic  processing.

2021 
1. 1.1 Lakh crore Loan Guarantee Scheme for COVID Affected Sectors which 
includes Rs. 50,000 crore for health sector to scale up medical infrastructure 
targeting under-served areas and Rs. 60,000 crore for other sectors. Interest  rate 
capped at 8.25% p.a. for other sectors and further decisions to be taken at later 
stage based on evolving needs. 
2. Additional 1.5 lakh crore for Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 
(ECLGS) launched as part of AtmaNirbhar Bharat Package in May, 2020.  Limit 
of admissible guarantee and loan amount increased above existing level of 20% 
of outstanding on each loan. Overall cap of admissible guarantee raised from Rs. 
3 lakh crore to Rs. 4.5 lakh crore. 
3. Extension of Atmanirbhar Bharat RozgarYojana Launched on 1st Oct, 2020. 
Scheme extended from 30.6.2021 to 31.03.2022. Incentivizes employers for 
creation of new employment, restoration of loss of employment through EPFO. 
Approved outlay Rs. 22,810 crore for 58.50 lakh estimated beneficiaries. Last 
date for re gistration is 30.06.2021. Subsidy provided for two years from 
registration for new employees drawing monthly wages less than Rs. 15000 for:  

 
 
51 
 
(i) Both Employer’s and Employee’s share of contribution (total 24% of wages) 
for establishment strength upto 1000 employees. 
(ii) Only Employee’s share (12% of wages) in case of establishment strength of 
more than 1000.

Corporation (ECGC) promotes exports by providing credit insurance services. 
Proposed to infuse equity in ECGC over 5 years to boost export insurance cover 
by Rs. 88,000 crore.

1. As credit facilities to MSME borrowers, extended under the emergency credit 
line guarantee scheme of GoI guaranteed by national credit guarantee trustee 
company (NCGTC), are backed by an unconditional and irrevocable guarantee 
provided by the GoI, member l ending institutions, viz., SCBs (including 
scheduled RRBs), NBFCs (including HFCs as eligible under the scheme) and 
AIFIs, permitted to assign  zero per cent risk weight on the credit facilities  
extended under the ECLGS scheme to the extent of guarantee cov erage. 
2. In view of the need to support viable MSME entities on account of the fallout of 
COVID-19, the scheme of one -time restructuring of loans to MSMEs without an 
asset classification downgrade, was extended where the borrower’s account was a 
‘standard as set’ as on March 1, 2020 and the aggregate exposure of banks and 
NBFCs was not more than Rs.25 crore. The restructuring had to be implemented 
by March 31, 2021, subject to certain conditions. 
3. Scheduled Commercial Banks allowed to deduct credit disbursed to new MSME 
borrowers from their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) for calculation of 
the cash reserve ratio. To further incentivize the inclusion of the MSMEs into the 
banking system, this  exemption, available for exposures up to Rs 25 lakh and 
credit disbursed up to October 1, is being allowed until December 31, 2021.  
4. Special liquidity facility of Rs 16,000 crore to Small Industries Development 
Bank of India (SIDBI) for on -lending/refinancing - To meet the funding 
requirements of small industries including MSMEs and to kick start the 
investment cycle with additional focus on smaller MSMEs and businesses 
including those in credit deficient and aspirational districts, the Reserve Bank 
extended to SIDBI refinance facilities of ₹15,000 crore in April 2020, ₹15,000 
crore in April 2021 and ₹16,000 crore in June 2021 at the repo rate.  
5. Restructuring of MSME Accounts under Resolution Framework 2.0: Individual

borrowers, small businesses and MSMEs hav ing aggregate exposure of up to Rs

equivalent of incremental credit disbursed by them up to the fortnight ending July 
31, 2020 as retail loans for automobiles, residential housing and loans to micro, 
small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), over and above the outstanding level of 
credit to these segments as at the end of the fortnight ending on January 31, 2020 
from their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) for maintenance of cash

CHAPTER – I 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
   
Recommendation/ Observation 
1. The Automobile Sector, due to its strong forward and backward linkages with 
several key segments of   the economy, occupies   a  prominent  place in   the fabric of 
Indian Economy. Since the number of vehicles exported in various segments is nowhere 
near the potential, exporting vehicles in a large scale would significantly contribute to 
employment generation, trade balance and economic growth of the country. The 
Committee therefore recommends that constructive steps should be taken by the 
Government to pro mote export of vehicles in various segments, particularly the BS -VI 
compliant vehicles, and their engine & spare parts to various countries across the globe, 
especially to Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia and West Asia where there is still 
huge potential for the global automobile companies operating from India. The Committee 
also recommends that the Government in coordination with the automobile companies 
should take appropriate steps   to explore the rural markets, particularly in Two Wheeler 
and Three  Wheeler segments that would contribute substantially for the growth of the 
Auto Sector. 
        (Para 30) 
Action Taken Replies 
 With regards to providing support to auto industry for enhancing exports , the 
following steps have been taken in this direction. 
i)          PLI scheme for the auto sector has been notified with an outlay of Rs 25,938 
crore to enhance the competitiveness of the industry and will help it attain higher 
foothold in exports.  
A number of schemes such as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural E mployment 
Guarantee Act (MNREGA), PradhanMantri Gram SadakYojana (PMGSY), and National 
Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) have been launched for the development of rural

agencies like A RAI.Self-certification is pertinent for various other parameters like 
endurance, consistent performance, warranty etc (except for CMVR requirement) and it is 
being done by automotive industry. During the COVID -19 pandemic, ARAI had carried 
out virtual/remo te testing services for industry, wherever feasible. Hence, separate 
provision for self-certification by OEM is not required.    
v)  a)  Section 32 of the income -tax Act, 1961 provides for deduction on account of 
depreciation on tangible assets and intangible assets acquired on or after the 1st April 1998 
which are owned wholly or partially by the assesse which are used wholly or exclusively 
for the purpose of business and profession while computing the income under the head 
„Profits and gains of business or profession.‟ 

 16 
b)         under the Act, assets of similar nature are grouped together as Block of assets and 
depreciation can be claimed only on the basis of written down value (WDV) method 
(except undertakings engaged in power generation or power distribution) 
c)         Clause (ii) of sub -section (1) of section 32 provides for the calculation of 
depreciation on block of assets at the percentage specified in the second column of assets 
which are used for the business or profession of the assesse during th e previous year. 
Rates of depreciation on motor cars has been prescribed under the heading “machinery 
and plant” in the second column of the Table in New Appendix of Rules 5. 
d)         Section 32 also provides that if asset acquired by assesse during the previous year 
is put to use for the purpose of business or profession for the period less than one hundred 
and eighty days in that previous year, the deduction under section 32 shall be restricted to 
fifty per cent of the amount calculated at the percentag e prescribed for that asset in the 
second column of the Table in new Appendix I of rules 5. 
Further, to incentivize the automobile sector, additional depreciation allowance 
was provided in case of motor vehicle which were acquired on or after 23 rd August 2019 
and before 31st March 2020 and put to use before 31st March 2020. 
In view of the above, it is clear that depreciation on any asset including motor 
vehicle is allowed only when it is put up to use for the purpose of business or profession 
during the pre vious year. Accordingly, the above mentioned proposal to allow the 6 
months depreciation in FY 2019 -20 for the vehicles purchased till 30.05.2020 is not 
feasible. However, it may be noted that depreciation will be available to these vehicles 
when they are put to use for the purpose of business or profession during the relevant 
previous year. 
vi)        There already exist certain exemption notification which provide BCD exemption 
on the goods imported for R&D purpose subject to certain conditions, for examp le- 
notification no. 50/1996 -customs and 51/1996 -customs. Subject to the fulfillment of the 
conditions mentioned therein, automobile companies can also avail the benefit under the 
said notifications. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
21. The Indian Auto Industry is highly dependent on automotive spare parts imported 
(around 27%) from China. However, due to the outbreak of corona virus, the component 
manufacturing units were shuttered down in China stalling the imports and subsequently 
affecting the whole value ch ain in India. Keeping in view programme     of  "Make  in  
India"  and  localized    production,    the Committee recommends that the Government 
should encourage and promote setting up of new automotive component manufacturing 
units/MSMEs to strengthen the economy and become a self-reliant country. 
        (Para 84) 
22. In the current Global scenario, the Committee observes that many of the countries 
are planning to pull out their manufacturing units from China and are looking for 
alternate lucrative and pro spective countries for re -location. Since India could be a 
preferred destination for foreign investment due to its sustained GDP growth, expanded 
robust market, enabling environment and transparent open policy regime, the Committee 

 17 
desires that the Governm ent should take all out efforts to seize this opportunity and turn 
the present adversity to a blessing in disguise. 
        (Para 85) 
Action Taken Replies 
Production Linked Incentive on Automobiles and Auto Components will give 
philip to Auto Companies and related industries.

CHAPTER–III 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE HAS NOT ACCEPTED THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
23. The Committee notes that the GST rates on ICE based vehi cles are at the highest 
slab of 28%. GST on all electrically operated vehicles is fixed at 5% to promote electric 
mobility. The Committee, therefore, feels that if GST rebates for EVs could be given for 
creating Public demand, there is scope for reducing G ST on ICE Vehicles also to spur its 
demand to overcome the present slump in the Automobile Sector. The cost of BS -VI 
vehicles is expected to be higher by 10-15% due to upgraded technology. To mitigate this 
cost increase, the Committee is of the view that a  reduced GST rate to 18% will bring 
down a sizeable amount in vehicle price creating more demand for newer vehicles. The 
increased sale due to the reduction in GST rate, will cover up the loss in GST revenue. 
        (Para 49) 
 
24. Further, there has been a consistent drop in the International Crude   oil prices, 
which can prove to be advantageous to the Government as the expected loss to the 
exchequer,  due to the  proposed  reduction  in GST slab in the Auto Sector, can be offset 
by the  crude oil price fall. The Committee  feels  that the slump in the crude oil price will 
translate into huge savings on imports for the Government, besides benefitting the 
industries that are dependent on crude oil and its derivatives. 
        (Para 50) 
 
25. The Committee rec ommends that the DHI may bring these observations of the 
Committee to the notice of GST Council for a quick and expeditious action thereof.  
                  (Para 51) 
 
26. Further, the Committee recommends that the Government may consider 
rationalization in GST rates on ICE vehicles based on their size, CC, Price Brackets, 
Seating Capacity etc. rather than having a fixed slab on all categories without distinction 
of Standard, Popular, Luxury etc. in order to raise the demand for newer vehicles. 
        (Para 52) 
 
27. The Committee desires that the Government may take measures to promote more 
Public Transportation in various cities beyond what is being done under FAME -II 
Scheme, augment spending on infrastructure building, including Road & Highways, 
Airports, Railways etc., reduction in GST rate on ICE vehicles etc. to boost demand for 
new vehicles in all segments. 
        (Para 77)

vehicles in order to make small and mid vehicles more affordable which in turn 
create demand and boost sales.  The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) being the

Recommendation/ Observation 
28. The Committee was informed by the Auto Industry Associations that the non  
availability of finance to consumers due to tightening of norms for retail financing by the 
Banks across the board in rural as well as urban areas has a ffected the growth of the 
Auto Industry Sector. This approach by banks has reduced the availability of finance to 
customers to go in for new vehicle purchase. Further, Banks are following CIBIL ratings 
in a very rigorous manner as a result of which the cus tomers are finding it difficult to get 
automobile loans. Most of the two wheeler customers are first time users and they don't 
have any CIBIL ratings or credit ratings. Moreover, the markets are shifting towards 
rural markets, where potential customers fin d in difficult for getting loans as they do not 
have any record of financial security, since they do not pay income tax. So with 
increasing stringent compliance measures, the rural customers find it difficult to avail 
finance from the banks for purchasing new vehicles. Earlier financing of about 85 -90 
percent was available but now it is limited to only 60 -70%. As per the submission 9f 
Department of Heavy Industry, amongst all the sectoral loans, NPAs are the least at 1.5 - 
2% for Auto Loans. The Committee n otes that majority of vehicle purchases are made 
through loans. The Auto loan is a secured loan as the vehicle itself is collateral. The 
Committee, therefore, finds no reason why the banks should be refusing auto loans to 
prospective consumers. The Committ ee, therefore, recommends that Department of 
Heavy Industry should take up the matter with Department of Financial Services for 
issuing required instructions to all banks throughout the country to adopt a liberal policy 
in sanctioning of vehicle loans subj ect to minimum regulations of fulfilling the eligibility 
condition.

consideration of the matter.

Rs.70,000 crore have been released for PSU banks recapitalization to improve liquidity 
situation. The Committee is pleased to note the action taken by the Government to 
strengthen the bank liquidity and believes that such a move will help PSU Banks to boost 
lending and improve liquidity situation. Further, the NBFCs  will be allowed to use 
Aadhar authenticated KYCs to take up credit which would further help them to lend more 
Auto Loans. The Committee hopes that this move  by the Ministry of Finance would bring 
some respite to the Auto buyers   in the  country and help improve the downturn in the 
Automobile Sector.

view that though banks have been facing various   challenges because of bad loans,

new and emerging technological areas instead of concentrating solely on the expensive

REPORT 
 
 India‟s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Sector has emerged as a 
vibrant, dynamic and progressive sector of the Indian economy over the last five decades. 
MSME Sector not  only play crucial role in providing large -scale employment 
opportunities at comparatively lower capital cost than large industries but also help 
industrialization of rural and backward areas of the country, thereby, reducing regional 
imbalances, assuring more equitable distribution of national income and resources.  
MSME Sector has  strong linkages to large indu stries as ancillary units and contributes 
significantly in the inclusive industrial development of the country . MSME Sector is also 
nurturing a culture of entrepreneurship among the people of the country, especially the 
youth thereby mitigating the problem of unemployment effectively. 
 
2. MSMEs are widely spread across the country in almost all the sectors. MSMEs are 
now widening their domain across various sectors of the economy, producing diverse 
range of products and services to meet demands of domestic as well as Global markets 
and also proving to be a boon for aspiring entrepreneurs in India.  As informed by the       
M/o of MSME, the MSME Sector is providing livelihood to around 11.10 crore people of 
the country. There are a round 6.34 crore MSMEs , which contributed 27 per cent to the 
Gross Domestic Product in the year Financial Year 2020 -21.The MSME Sector has the 
huge potential to generate employment and livelihood in the rural hinterlands  of the 
country. It also has the capacity to earn foreign exchange for the exchequer through larger 
exports. 
 
3. COVID-19 pandemic had an enormous adverse impact on almost all sectors of the 
Indian economy including the MSME Sector, due to factors such as lack of funds, supply 
chain disruptions, lower productivity, non -availability of workforce etc. However, t he 
Government has adopted a multi -pronged approach covering the six pillars such as (i) 
New Enterprise Development and Employment Generation (ii) Credit Assistance and 
Capital Infusion (iii) Technological U pgradation (iv) Infrastructure & Capacity Building 
(v) Skill Development & Entrepreneurship Development T raining and (vi) Procurement 
and Marketing Support, in order to help the MSMEs to revive and regain their               
pre-pandemic growth trajectory as well as improve their economic growth. 

2 
 
Ministry of MSME  
 
4. The Ministry of MSME was formed on 9 th May, 2007 merging the erstwhile 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries and the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.  The 
Ministry designs policies, promotes/facilitates programmes/projects/schemes and 
monitors their implementation, with a view to assisting MSMEs and helping them to scale 
up.  
 
The major Schemes of the Ministry of MSME are mentioned as under:- 
 Prime Minister‟s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP); 
 Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA); 
 Interest Subsidy and Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme; 
 Strengthening of Infrastructure of Existing Weak Khadi Institutions and Assistance 
for Marketing Infrastructure; 
 Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); 
 A Scheme for Promoting Innovation and Rural Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE); 
 Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI); 
 Micro and Small Enterprises–Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP); 
 Science & Technology (S&T); 
 Honey Mission;  
 Kumbhar Shashaktikaran Programme; 
 The National Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Hub;  
 Scheme for Promotion of MSMEs in NE Region and Sikkim; and 
 Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line (GECL). 
 
New Definition of MSMEs 
 
5. The Committee was informed that the revision in the definition of MSMEs  which 
was brought in w.e.f. 1stJuly, 2020 as part of the AtmaNirbhar Bharat package introduced 
a composite  criteria of investment and annual turnover and identical limits for 
manufacturing and services sector ( table below). The resulting economies of scale can 
enhance productivity without the MSMEs losing out on several Government incentives 
including market support, export promotion, preferential procurement in the public sector 
and incentives through the Micro Small  Enterprises-Cluster Development Programme 
(MSE-CDP), Prime Minister Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) and Scheme 
of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) and enabling of IT

ecosystems. This enabling environment will promote compet ition among MSMEs .The 
new definition of MSMEs is as under:-

6. The Committee understands that the modified definition of MSMEs will 
facilitate expansion and growth of MSME enterprises , increasing the investment 
limit under the new definition allows MSMEs to invest in plant an d machinery for 
growth without the fear of losing the status.  Further, the increased limit also enables 
MSMEs to invest in new technologies to enhance their productivity.  It also removes 
the distinction between MSMEs in the manufacturing as well as services sector and 
increases the country’s exports through MSMEs. The Committee appreciates the 
Government’s decision to modify the definition of M icro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises as detailed above at para no.  5, as per the long -standing demand of 
Industry Associations.  The Committee also welcomes the decision to include retail 
and wholesale trade under the purview of MSME, thereby enabling them to get 
priority sector lending.  
 
Demands for Grants (2022-23) 
 
7. Regarding the details of the Action Plan set for the Ministry for the year2022 -23, 
the Committee was informed by the Ministry that an amount of Rs. 21,422crore has been 
allocated to the Ministry of MSME for the year 2022 -23. The Action Plan of the Ministry 
focuses on strengthening the overall ecosyst em of MSMEs by providing infrastructural 
support, marketing avenues, proper access to finance,  technical support and capacity 
building etc. This action plan is broadly reflected in the Output -Outcome Monitoring 
Framework Document of the Ministry for FY 2022-23.  
9. During the course of the presentation in connection with DFG (2022 -23), the 
Ministry of MSME apprised the Committee about the main highlights of the Union 
Budget 2022-23 for MSME Sector, which is as under :- 
 
 Udyam, e-shram, NCS and ASEEM portals to be interlinked; 
 ECLGS to be extended up to March 2023;

9. The Committee notes that for the Financial Year 2022-23, the M/o MSME has 
been allocated Rs. 21422 crore as BE against the projection of Rs. 24979.6 crore 
which translates to 85.76%.  Therefore, there is a shortfall of Rs. 3557.6 crore  in BE 
allocation.  The SME division has been allocated Rs. 200 crore against the demanded 
amount of Rs. 208 crore , which comes to 96.15%.  However, the Committee notes 
that allocation to both DC -MSME and ARI Division of the Ministry has been 
curtailed substantially as DC-MSME has got 88.99% whereas A RI Division got only 
72.73% of the projected amount.  Both ARI Division and O/o DC -MSME are the 
backbone of the Ministry of MSME and are therefore crucial for development and 
growth of MSME sector.  The Committee understands that O/o DC -MSME 
implements poli cies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure 
and support services to MSMEs whereas ARI Division looks after the administration 
of KVIC, COIR Board, MGIRI, besides supervising flagship schemes of the Ministry 
such as PMEGP, SFURUTI, ASPIRE, etc.  Therefore, inadequate allocation of funds 

5 
 
would jeopardise the smooth functioning of the Ministry  and successful 
implementation of its schemes/projects.  The Committee , therefore,  recommends 
that the M/o MSME should impress upon the Ministry of Finance to get enhanced 
budget allocation for both ARI Division and O/o DC-MSME at RE stage.

12. The Committee notes that for financial year 2021 -22, the Ministry was 
allocated Rs. 15699.65 crore as BE and RE and the AE upto 31 st January, 2022 
stands at Rs. 12071.84 crore which is only 76.89% of the allocated BE/RE.  
Therefore, the Committee expects the Ministry to utilize the balance amount of 
23.11% during the remaining two months.  Further, the Ministry should henceforth 
rationalize the expenditure spreading all through the year to avoid uneven spending 
 
13. The Committee further observes that for the FY 2022 -23, the Ministry has 
been allocated Rs. 21,422 crore as BE,  which apparently appears to be a significant 
increase from the previous year's BE of Rs. 15 ,699.65 crore .  However, out of Rs. 
21,422 crore, Rs. 15,000 crore  has been  earmarked for Guaranteed Emergency 
Credit Line scheme (GECL) leaving behind Rs. 6,422 crore only, which is the actual 
allocation for development of other schemes/projects of the Ministry . BE allocation 
of Rs. 6422 crore for FY 2022 -23  as mentioned at paragraph number 1 0 above  is 
the lowest allocation as compared to past several years’ i.e. BE 2017 -18, 2018 -19, 
2019-20 and 2020 -21.  The Committee expresses concern on such poor allocation of 
BE 2022 -23 to the M/o MSME especially at this juncture when MSME sector is 
struggling to revive from the huge adverse impact of COVID -19 Pandemic and 
remain in operation due to liquidity crunch.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should address the issue by taking it up with the            
M/o Finance for an enhanced allocation at the RE stage to enable the Ministry to 
achieve its vision of a progressive MSME sector by promoting growth and 
development of the Sector, through support to existing enterprises, adopting cutting 
edge technologies, encouraging creation of new enterprises etc. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry should utilize the BE 2022 -23 of Rs. 21422.00 crore 
optimally for the development of MSME Sector. 
 
14. Further with regard to SME Division the RE 2021 -22 and AE upto  31st 
January, 2022, are Rs. 208.6 5 crore and Rs. 146.6 crore respectively , which shows 
that the Ministry have utilized only 70.26% of the RE.  As regards ARI Division, the 
RE 2021 -22 stands at Rs. 4202.73 crore whereas AE upto 31 st January, 2022 is          
Rs. 2519.76 crore , which is only 59.95% of RE . The fund utilization by the               
O/o DC-MSME is slightly promising as compared to SME and ARI Divisions, as the 
O/o DC-MSME has spent 83.32% of RE 2021 -22. The Committee suggests that the 
Ministry of MSME should strive hard to utilize the remaining amount of RE 

10 
 
allocated to all the three aforesaid wings of the Ministry optimally so that the  
schemes/projects do not suffer for lack of funds. 
 
15. The Committee also notes that RE and AE for Distressed Asset Fund – 
Subordinate Debt for Stressed MSMEs for 2020 -21 were Rs. 227.41 crore  &                
Rs. 157.41 crore respectively and BE, RE &  AE for the scheme in FY 2021 -22 were 
Rs. 300 crore, Rs. 1.00 crore and Nil respectively.  Now, for FY 2022 -23 a BE of         
Rs. 100 crore has been allocated.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
reasons for such deviation in outalys of the scheme.    
 
 
Views/Suggestions of the Stakeholders 
 
 
16. As part of examination of the DFG (2022 -23), t he Committee had sought the 
views/suggestions of the Associations (FICCI, FISME, CII and ASSOCHAM) on the 
Government‟s target of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises contributing $2 trillion to 
the country‟s target of becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 . The Associations apprised 
the Committee that although the Covid pandemic had adversely affected the MSME 
Sector but they are very optimistic that MSME Sector will revive quickly but it is very 
important that the blueprint laid down by the Government materializes in a time -bound 
manner. The important suggestions put forth by the Associations in this regard along with 
the recommendations of the Committee are as under:- 
 
SEPARATE POLICY FOR MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
17. Issues of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises are different from each other and  
unified policy would not be able to treat them well as per their actual requirements.  The 
schemes need to be segregated and modified as per each of the category so that  every 
category has specific solutions. It will help enterprises to identify schemes, which are 
relevant for them. Medium sector enterprises have the potential to grow to become large 
enterprises and subsequently, these enterprises could support many other Micro & Small 
enterprises in cascading effect. If only 10% of medium enterprises could be  transformed 
into large enterprises, there would be a significant cascading effect for Micro and Small 
enterprises. Therefore, separate policy should be formulated  for Medium enterprises. At 
present, no significant scheme is  available for Medium Enterprises and given that new 

11 
 
definition is into effect, announcing special schemes for medium -sized enterprises would 
benefit numerous enterprises who have joined MSME spectre due to new definition. 
 
18. The Committee recommends that based on the divergent needs of the Medium 
Enterprises vis-à-vis Small and Micro Enterprises, it is in interest of both the 
categories to have separate and dedicated policies for better targeted development 
and growth. 
 
SETTING UP OF SME FINANCE COMPANIES 
 
19. At present, no SME Finance Companies exist in the country. Therefore, as in the 
case of infrastructure finance companies or micro-finance companies that are not engaged 
in real economic activity  but in the financing of it, SME finance  companies may  be 
established in the country. 
 
20. The Committee suggest s that SME finance companies may be established in 
the country on the lines of infrastructure finance companies or micro -finance 
companies that are not engaged in real economic activity but in financing of it. 
 
CONSULTATION WITH STAKEHOLDERS 
 
21. There is an absence of a structured need assessment  exercise before proposing and 
designing any of the major schemes. Due to weak stakeholder discussions on proposed 
schemes, the design flaws come to light too late and  also discourage potential 
implementing agencies. There is a special need for the involvement of stakeholders at the 
design stage of the  scheme to make the schemes demand driven, especially the schemes 
that are based  on SPV/consortium approach. Process of structured need assessment will 
help generate „content‟ having clarity on objectives, beneficiaries; scope and coverage of  
schemes; role and function of implementing agency. 
22. The Committee is of the view that Emphasis should be made on involvement 
of stakeholders at design stage of schemes, especially the schemes that are based on 
SPV/Consortium approach. 
GST REGIME 
 
23. The GST regime was meant to be a digitized system; however, department 
authorities still insist that separate hard copies are also provided to claim refund. This 
defeats the  purpose of digitizing process. The time involved by the MSMEs in finally 

12 
 
getting the  refund sanctioned causes a tremendous strain on the cash flows of the 
MSMEs, which in turn restricts the possibility of increasing exports. 
 
24. The Committee recommends that the GST regime should be a digitized 
system, without the requirement o f separate hard copies to be provided the 
concerned Dep artment to claim refund. This not only defeats the purpose of 
digitizing process, bu t also eases inordinate delay in getting the refund sanctioned , 
thereby resulting in tremendous strain on cash flows of the MSMEs. 
 
EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE GUARANTEE SCHEME (ECLGS) 
 
25. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme mandated for providing collateral 
free loans to MSMEs has been a very effective financial measure to restore their liquidity 
and financial health. The said emergency credit line has greatly helped MSMEs to restart 
operations by giving them additional working capital support. It is a welcome step of the 
Government in the Budget 2022 -23 to increase the corpus of ECLGS to Rs. 5 lakh crore 
by adding  Rs. 50 thousand crore for hospitality & related enterprises and extend the 
validity of scheme till 31st March, 2023. However, some more concerns have been raised 
by MSME, which are not able to avail the scheme. Repayment period of 3 -4 years 
including moratorium period under the scheme is very little time for MSMEs which are 
struggling to survive through second wave of Covid -19. As the cash  flow has dried, it 
would take a longer period to come back to normal liquidity and hence it is suggested that  
repayment period should be extended up to 7 – 8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium 
on principal amount. With respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 
onwards should be announced by the RBI. This accumulative interest  should be made part 
of term loan/principal amount. No interest on interest should be charged from MSMEs 
while amalgamating the interest in principal amount. 
 
26. The Committee finds that under Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme, 
repayment period of 3 -4 years including moratorium period is a very short period 
for MSMEs, which are struggling to survive from the second wave of Covid -19. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the repayment period should be extended 
upto 7 -8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium on principal amount. With 

13 
 
respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 onwards should be 
announced by RBI. 
 
 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND TRUST FOR MICRO AND SMALL 
ENTERPRISES (CGTMSE) 
 
27. During the budget 2022-23, it was announced by the Hon‟ble Finance Minister that 
the CGTMSE Scheme shall be revamped and Rs. 2 lakh crore will also be infused in the  
scheme. It is indeed a welcome step in the direction to make this scheme more viable  and 
convenient for its stakeholders including MSEs. As the scheme is to be revamped,  it has 
been requested that the limit of collateral free loans under this scheme, either term loan or 
working capital loan, should be increased from existing Rs. 2 crore to upto Rs. 5 crores, 
irrespective of the constitution (Private Ltd ., LLP, Partnership and/or proprietorship) of 
applicant MSEs provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
28. The Committee is in consonance with the suggestion of Associations and 
recommends that while revamping the CGTMSE scheme, the limit of collateral free 
loans under this scheme, either term loan or working capital loan should be 
increased from the existing R s. 2 crore upto Rs. 5 crores, irrespective of the 
Constitution (Private Ltd., LLP, Partnership and/or Proprietorship) of applicant 
MSE’s provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
AATMANIRBHAR BHARAT 
 
29. Government is focusing upon Make in India, which is entirely appreciable effort as 
it helps MSMEs to grow. It is a fact that India is importing MSME oriented products in  
huge quantity, which can be manufactured in India. One of the reasons behind this  could 
be explained as lack of awareness amongs t MSMEs about the products that are  being 
imported in the country. Feedback has been received from the industry that  Government 
should put out a list of such products along with their production  specifications so that 
enterprises become excited about getting into the production of such products. Such 
imported products should also carry the information about their  market potential in the 
country. This would be beneficial for a large number of potential entrepreneurs who wish 
to set up new manufacturing enterprises. A Central Market  Intelligence Center for import 

14 
 
related products and components would be of great  help to MSMEs to achieve the goal of 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat. Soft loans at minimal  interest rate of 3 -4% with a minimum tenure 
of 9-10 years for repayment period, Easy land acquisition, less compliances could be key 
factors in developing domestic manufacturing with MSMEs. Till the domestic 
manufacturing is strengthened, high  import restrictions should be avoided and only, if 
necessary, it should be applied in phased manner. 
 
30. The Committee understands that a number of MSME oriented products are 
presently being imported , which can be manufactured in India. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that a Central Market Intelligence Centre for import related 
products and components be set up in the country. The said Centre may be 
entrusted with the task of putting out a list of products , which are being imported 
alongwith their specificat ions and spreading awareness of the same through 
electronic, print and social media to attract interested entrepreneurs to set up new 
manufacturing enterprises in MSME Sector, thereby fulfilling the Government ’s 
vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat. 
 
TESTING AND CERTIFICATION FACILITIES IN TECHNOLOGY CENTRES  
31. For any business to flourish, it is important that products are of certain standards 
and excel in quality. For exports, MSMEs need to meet a certain required international or  
regional specific standard for which adequate facilities are not available in the country. 
Besides, available testing facilities are costly , which MSMEs cannot afford. Testing &  
Certifications should be made convenient and cheaper for MSMEs. The country has 
arobust infrastructure of  technology centers that are supporting MSMEs in many ways.  
The Associations have received very positive feedback about these technology centers 
and Ministry of MSME must be congratulated for running this facility across the country. 
Keeping this network i n view, suggestion s have also been received that Technology 
Centers could also be utilised to facilitate subsidised testing for regional  MSMEs. A 
mechanism/tie-up should be developed that testing can be done in India at these 
technology Centers whereas cer tificates for the same test could be issued from  various 
global testing centers , which are acceptable in respective countries/regions.  Ministry of 
MSME could do tie-ups with various global agencies through its technology centers.  
 
32. The Committee recommends that the existing Technology Centres should also 
be used to facilitate subsidi sed testing and certification of regional MSMEs. Further 

15 
 
a mechanism should be devised by the Ministry to tie up with global Testing Centres 
whose certificates are acceptable in respective countries/regions. The Committee 
hopes that this new arrangement will not only ease the testing process and reduce 
the cost, but also encourage new entrepreneurs to come up with more innovations.

working capital (working cycle) @ 16 months but on the other hand the banks are 
calculating it at 4 months and this is the bone of contention between KVIC and 
banks, which appears to be one of the lacuna e for the gap existing between ISEC 
issued and Bank finance .  T he Committee observes that this issue needs to be 
addressed at the appropriate level.  The Committee strongly recommends that a n 
amicable formula may be devised by KVIC and banks, which is acceptable to both 
in order to increase the efficiency and efficacy of the ISEC scheme.

Scheme to increase the off take .  The procedures may be simplified, formalities may 
be kept at minimum, and banks may be educated about the Scheme and advised t o

claims.
